title: 'It's offensively cheap': How solar power is quietly becoming bigger than nuclear
content:
'It's offensively cheap': How solar power is quietly becoming bigger than nuclear
20 hours ago
Share
Save
Add as preferred on Google
Jocelyn Timperley
Getty Images
(Credit: Getty Images)
After defying projections, solar's dramatic growth means it is now overtaking nuclear as a global power source. Here are seven reasons for solar's success, and where it might go from here.
The world's solar power is crossing a threshold. A decade ago, it barely registered on a global scale, providing just 1% of the world's power. In 2026, it will almost certainly increase to 10% of power, and overtake nuclear, a mainstay of electricity since the late 1970s.
Globally, solar electricity generation quietly overtook nuclear power (just) in 2025, according to statistics from UK-based energy think tank Ember. And BBC analysis of Ember data over the past 12 months up to September 2026 shows it clearly outstripping nuclear, producing 13% more power.
"[Solar] generating more electricity than all the world's nuclear power plants is a pretty insane stat, for sure," says Dave Jones, co-founder of Ember. 
From China's vast arrays to a recent solar upsurge driven by escalating oil prices, the incredible rise of solar power has defied all projections. Here are seven ways it has become an apparently "unstoppable force" – and what the future looks like from here.
ADVERTISEMENT
1. An underestimated force 
"Solar is now the engine of the power transition," says Jan Rosenow, a professor of energy and climate policy at the University of Oxford in the UK.
Solar has become the fastest-growing source of new electricity in history, and by far the largest source of new electricity globally. In 2025, it met three-quarters of the growth in the world's demand for electricity, overtaking wind power generation (wind power is also growing, just a little more slowly).
That's where solar's going, to not just be king of electricity, but king of energy – Dave Jones
"It wasn't expected," says Rosenow. Mainstream projections, he says, have underestimated solar year after year. Outlooks such as those from the International Energy Agency (IEA), an influential intergovernmental organisation based in Paris, "assumed linear growth and slowly falling costs, and got both wrong".
Over 2026, multiple sources indicate solar electricity generation will almost certainly far exceed nuclear globally. Nuclear's electricity generation has remained more or less constant since 2000, while solar's has increased some 2,700-fold.
Ember/ BBC
Ember data shows solar electricity generation narrowly surpassing nuclear in 2025. In 2026, it will almost certainly well exceed it (Credit: Ember/BBC)
2. 'Offensively cheap'
Solar, a mature technology for some 15 years now, became the cheapest electricity in history in 2020. Since then, solar has scaled, efficiency has risen, and the amount of silicon and silver used in panels has gone down, leading prices to fall yet further, says Jones. 
"Massive Chinese manufacturing scale and current overcapacity have pushed module prices to record lows," says Rosenow. 
In particular, a large fall in the price of panels in 2023-24 pushed us into the current era of what Jones calls "offensively cheap" solar. "A panel in itself is just so unbelievably cheap," he says. "It's well under $100 (£75)… and that's going to keep you generating electricity for 30, 40 years without any input at all."
Of course, it's not just in purely economic terms that solar is bringing down costs. Researchers have calculated the US's rising wind and solar generation brought it $249bn (£186bn) in climate and health benefits between 2019 and 2022.
3. Global uptake
China is still the world's biggest solar power by far but is by no means the only player.
Despite the US imposing a variety of tariffs on solar, it remains the second country when it comes to installations, which are still skyrocketing – especially in states won by President Trump in 2024. In fact, the US now has enough solar to power more than one-third of its households.
"Tariffs and other federal policies that constrain renewable energy growth are certainly expected to raise costs and slow expansion relative to what we otherwise would have seen," says Alicia Zhao, an expert in US mitigation pathways at the University of Maryland. 
"However, economics are a key part of why solar has been able to grow so quickly. Even with rising costs, solar is still one of the cheapest sources of new power in the US. And it is getting built regardless of political lines."
Getty Images
China's internal solar boom is now slowing down, but its cheap solar exports to other countries are still increasing (Credit: Getty Images)
India, meanwhile, is moving away from fossil fuels far faster than China did, and new solar has met 60% of its rise in power demand in the past two years.
In Australia, over four million homes now have rooftop solar: well over a third of all households.
4. Unreliable fossil fuels
Countries like Pakistan and Lebanon have also begun installing solar at breakneck speeds, while across Africa countries are installing some 100,000 solar panels per day.
In many places, escalating diesel prices, driven by the Russia-Ukraine conflict and US-Israel war with Iran, has swung the cost needle yet further in solar's favour. This is especially the case in many African countries where home diesel generators are a mainstay due to unreliable grids. Rooftop solar panels, nearly all of them imported from China, have now taken off as an alternative.
Ethiopia has even banned the import of petrol and diesel cars in a bid to tackle oil dependency and pollution, says Jones.
Solar is also rapidly providing new electricity where fossil-based grids can't keep up with demand. Pakistan, for example, has become a surprising poster child for the solar revolution due to its extraordinarily rapid rise in installations. In 2019, solar provided less than 2% of its electricity; now it's 24%, driven by costly, unreliable grid electricity combined and cheap solar imports from China.
"What's really incredible in Pakistan is… generally most of the solar boom has been out of people's pockets," says Jones. "People can afford it, without needing to take out loans."
A similar story has been seen in several other "sun belt" countries, from Lebanon to Nigeria. "[Solar] lets households act without waiting for governments or utilities," says Rosenow. "In uncertain times, that speed and independence is extremely valuable."
5. Battery revolution
Solar power, of course, can only be produced during the day when the sun is shining. To turn it into electricity that can be dispatched at any time, it needs to be paired with batteries.
Fortunately, batteries have been having their own cost revolution, transforming their ability to support the solar rollout. "Solar plus storage is now routinely cheaper than new fossil plants in sunny regions," says Rosenow. "Batteries have largely solved the daily problem of shifting midday sun into the evening."
Alamy
Solar has gone from Pakistan's fifth-largest electricity source in 2023 to its largest in 2025, says Rosenow (Credit: Alamy)
In California, for example, solar and batteries met on average over a quarter of electricity demand from 19:00-21:00 (the evening peak) over the first half of 2026. US states such as Vermont are now rolling out grid-integrated systems of home batteries, often paired with solar.
Barriers still remain for longer-term storage of solar across seasons, cloudy periods and monsoon seasons, though, both Rosenow and Jones say. It means the integration of solar into the wider electricity system still matters, says Rosenow.
6. Electrify everything
Solar is seen as a key part of the push towards electrification, reducing fossil fuel use in areas that previously didn't use electricity, such as via electric cars. Electrification has been chosen as a major theme at this year's UN climate talks in Turkey.
"That's where solar's going, to not just be king of electricity, but king of energy," says Jones. 
Still, it all requires a plan, Julia Souder, chief executive of the Long Duration Energy Storage Council, a global executive-led non-profit established at COP26, warned recently. "There is an inherent danger in uncontrolled electrification, and adding massive new loads without built-in flexibility creates a fragile system," she wrote in a blog for international policy network Ren21. "Electrification is not automatically resilient." 
The limits on solar are now grids, storage and how fast we electrify demand, says Rosenow – not panels or cost. "The bigger question is no longer whether solar grows but whether our power systems and institutions can keep up."
In the US, data centres and electrification mean power demand is growing for the first time in decades, says Zhao, with energy security a national priority. 
"Renewables already make up over 90% of new capacity in the US," she says. "This need for secure, quickly deployable electricity could create a critical opportunity for [further] renewable energy growth even without support from the current federal government."
7. Expanding tech
In the past few years, plug-in panels (or "balcony solar"), have started spreading rapidly in Germany. These generate less electricity than rooftop panels but feed it directly into homes via a standard socket.
They have now been approved in several other countries and US states including California.
Meanwhile, agrivoltaics, which combines food production and solar panels, is being touted as a solution to concerns in some areas about the land use of solar.
Getty Images
In Kentucky, US, a solar ranch pays a local farmer to graze his sheep among its solar panels, producing pasture-fed meat while keeping grass and weeds down (Credit: Getty Images)
Other technologies from floating and "mirror" solar plants to perovskite panels and solar windows could all see growth in coming years.
What's next for solar
In 2026, the world's solar capacity will go on rising, but the rate of expansion may slow down for the first time ever, says Jones.
This is down to China: last summer, it changed its regime for managing and supporting new solar installations, leading to a burst of installations in 2025 to fall under the old price regime. Elsewhere, it's a different picture. "If you exclude China, there's more panels being installed this year than last year," says Jones.
By 2030, the IEA thinks solar power generation will have reached double that of 2025's levels, with solar overtaking hydro to become the world's third-largest electricity source.
"Wherever grid power is costly and unreliable, the economics keep pulling people towards solar," says Rosenow. "There is one caveat: if Chinese solar panels are difficult to import this will not happen at speed." 
More like this:
• The US state replacing power plants with home batteries
• The dream of beaming solar energy from orbit
• Perovskite: The 'wonder material' that could transform solar 
There has been a lot of bad news about the climate recently. It's now incredibly likely the 1.5C global limit set in Paris in 2015 will be breached, the world is seeing rising climate impacts and is edging towards several climate tipping points this century.
But the solar success story shows we are also making progress in ways that were never anticipated. A decade ago, "no one was getting close to expecting that to happen", says Jones, noting that the growth in clean electricity has directly translated to fewer coal plants being built. 
"Now, worst cases [of climate change] are somewhere between 2-3C of warming, rather than 4C of warming."

Apple gives iPad mini its biggest update ever - Apple
content:
PRESS RELEASE
October 26, 2026
Apple gives iPad mini its biggest update ever
Featuring a stunning OLED display in an even thinner and lighter design, a huge leap in performance, faster wireless connectivity, and water and dust resistance
The new iPad mini offers the full iPad experience users can hold in the palm of their hand.
CUPERTINO, CALIFORNIA Apple today unveiled the all-new iPad mini, featuring a stunning OLED display in an even thinner and lighter design, a huge leap in performance with A20 Pro, and water and dust resistance.1 The larger 8.5-inch OLED display, also available with a nano-texture option, delivers higher contrast and more than 2x higher peak brightness than the previous-generation iPad mini for a brilliant and immersive viewing experience.2 A20 Pro supercharges AI with Neural Accelerators in each GPU core and Dual 16-core Neural Engine. iPad mini now has a 12MP Center Stage front camera on the landscape edge that’s perfect for video calls, an innovative Acoustic Display for an even better audio experience, faster wireless and cellular connectivity, and fast-charge support.3 With its incredible set of advanced features, it’s the most capable and versatile iPad mini ever.
The new iPad mini is powered by iPadOS 27 with the next generation of Apple Intelligence and Siri AI, which can draw on a user’s personal context to help them find what they need, answer questions on virtually any topic with broad world knowledge, and understand what’s on their screen.4 The combination of powerful features and game-changing iPadOS 27 capabilities makes the new iPad mini a compelling value. Customers can pre-order it along with the new Smart Folio starting Wednesday, October 28, with availability beginning Friday, November 6.
“iPad mini is beloved for its fantastic portability, performance, and display by a wide range of users, from creators and small business owners to doctors, field service workers, and gamers,” said Dave Pakula, Apple’s vice president of Hardware Engineering. “With a remarkably thinner and lighter design, a stunning new OLED display, the incredibly powerful A20 Pro, and water and dust resistance, the new iPad mini is a huge leap forward for users who love having the full iPad experience in the palm of their hand.”
Thinner and Lighter Than Ever
At 5.4 mm thin, the new iPad mini is more portable than ever, and is available in two gorgeous finishes: a new midnight and a beautiful starlight. Remarkably thinner and lighter than the previous generation, iPad mini is now even easier to carry, whether a user is reading, working on the go, or using it with one hand. It also features an IP67 rating to protect against water and dust — ideal for a range of use cases, such as working outside on a rainy day or reading by the pool.1
A Stunning OLED Display
The new iPad mini comes with a stunning OLED display that delivers amazing front-of-screen performance and an even larger 8.5-inch size while maintaining the same footprint as the previous mini, thanks to 24 percent thinner bezels.2 The Super Retina XDR display features OLED technology to deliver pixel-level lighting control for much deeper blacks and support for the P3 wide color gamut for more vivid and accurate imagery.
For an even better visual experience across a range of lighting conditions, iPad mini also features peak brightness of up to 1200 nits — more than 2x higher than the previous generation — and supports 600 nits of full-screen brightness for SDR and HDR content, along with a 2,000,000:1 contrast ratio. And with a 1-nit minimum brightness, iPad mini is even more suitable for dim environments, from users reading in bed at night to pilots checking their electronic flight bag in the cockpit. iPad mini also offers a new nano-texture display option, which users love on iPad Pro, that reduces glare in bright environments — ideal for creatives editing outdoors or technicians working in the field. Together, these display advancements extend the versatility of iPad mini across an even wider range of use cases.
A Huge Leap in Performance
A20 Pro delivers a giant leap in performance for iPad mini, significantly boosting graphics and AI-intensive tasks. It is built using Apple’s latest 2-nanometer process technology and a new package inspired by M-series chips. Powered by a 7-core GPU with Neural Accelerators in each GPU core, iPad mini delivers up to 4.5x faster AI performance than the previous generation — perfect for AI tasks ranging from running on-device models in creative apps to running local LLMs.3 And with the latest graphics architecture, including dynamic caching and hardware-accelerated mesh shading and ray tracing, graphics performance jumps by up to 2.7x — great for gaming and 3D rendering.3 A20 Pro also features up to a 6-core CPU for up to 60 percent faster multithreaded performance for everyday tasks like editing photos and working across apps.3
The 512GB configuration features a powerful Dual 16-core Neural Engine, which offers double the processing power of the previous generation, accelerating tasks in apps like Draw Things and Detail. By engaging all 32 cores, A20 Pro becomes a powerhouse for more advanced on-device AI workloads. A20 Pro also brings over a 2x increase in unified memory bandwidth, unlocking additional performance for new levels of capability and responsiveness across graphics and AI-intensive workloads.
A Rich New Audio Experience and Advanced Cameras
The new iPad mini features an innovative Acoustic Display for an even better audio experience when gaming, watching videos, or editing content. Specially designed woofers are paired through the display to produce punchier bass and more volume. In addition, custom tweeters are now hidden between the glass and aluminum enclosure for clearer highs. The Acoustic Display also features a sealed enclosure that helps iPad mini achieve its IP67 rating.
The 12MP Center Stage front camera is now on the landscape edge, perfect for FaceTime calls, video conferencing, and collaboration. And the 12MP Wide back camera captures gorgeous photos with Smart HDR 4 and 4K video at up to 60 fps, while the addition of an Adaptive True Tone flash improves photos and makes document scanning better than ever.
N1 and C2 Come to iPad mini
iPad mini now features N1, an Apple-designed wireless networking chip that enables Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and Thread.5 N1 brings better performance when connected to 5GHz Wi-Fi networks and improves the overall performance and reliability of features like AirDrop and AirPlay.6
Cellular models of the new iPad mini feature C2, Apple’s next-generation cellular modem system. C2 enables up to 50 percent faster cellular data speeds compared to the previous generation of iPad mini, with even greater power efficiency.6 And with iPadOS 27, moving between cellular and Wi-Fi networks is more seamless than ever, so users can stay connected on a FaceTime call even while they’re in transit. Users can also enjoy the benefits of eSIM, which lets them quickly and securely add a new plan, connect and transfer existing plans digitally, and stay in touch with family and friends regardless of Wi-Fi availability.7
iPadOS 27 with the Next Generation of Apple Intelligence and Siri AI
iPad mini users can get even more done with Siri AI, rolling out in beta with iPadOS 27. Siri AI is an entirely new version of Siri, powered by Apple Intelligence, that is profoundly more personal, capable, and conversational.4 iPad mini also supports Apple’s most advanced on-device model ever, for even more expressive voices with Siri AI as well as a major boost in accuracy with systemwide dictation.
Siri AI can draw on personal context understanding to help users find what they need in the moment across their personal messages, emails, photos, and more; use onscreen awareness to take action related to the content on a user’s screen; and answer questions about virtually any topic. Additionally, Apple Intelligence makes apps smarter and more useful. Users can improve a photo’s composition after it’s been taken using tools such as upgraded Clean Up, Spatial Reframing, and Extend. And now the all-new Image Playground app offers photorealistic imagery. In Safari, Notify Me helps users monitor web pages for changes, like product restocks or price drops, and stay on top of updates. Apple Intelligence uses on-device processing and Private Cloud Compute to help protect users’ privacy. When Private Cloud Compute is handling users’ requests, their personal data is not stored nor made accessible to Apple or anyone else.
iPadOS 27 also delivers an expansive set of improvements that make iPad more responsive, reliable, and easy to use, along with updates to Liquid Glass, including a new slider in Settings that gives users the option to personalize it, adjusting it anywhere from ultraclear to fully tinted to match their preference. With iPadOS 27.2, iPad mini also supports extended display mode when connected to an external display, great for users multitasking with windowed apps.
Additionally, powerful and easy-to-use tools help parents manage what their kids can see, who they can talk to, and when they have access to apps. For parents and families looking for more information on how to help create safer, more enriching digital experiences for their kids, Apple also has a website with details on the latest tools and how to get started using them.
Accessories That Unlock More Ways to Be Productive and Creative
The new Smart Folio features a two-panel architecture, offering a slim, lightweight cover that magnetically attaches to iPad mini.8 Crafted with TechWoven fabric in navy blue and taupe to complement the iPad mini finishes, the Smart Folio has an adjustable design that gives users a greater range of motion, including new viewing angles, for enhanced versatility.
iPad mini supports both Apple Pencil (USB-C) and Apple Pencil Pro, giving users two incredible options to bring their ideas to life.8 Apple Pencil (USB-C) is a great value for everyday tasks like note-taking and sketching, while Apple Pencil Pro delivers industry-leading capabilities for the ultimate pencil experience. With Apple Pencil Pro, users can take advantage of innovative features like squeeze and barrel roll to work in entirely new ways, as well as utilize Find My support to help locate it when misplaced.
iPad mini and the Environment
iPad mini was built with the environment in mind and drives progress toward Apple’s ambitious plan to be carbon neutral across its entire footprint by 2030. It is made with 35 percent recycled content overall,9 including 100 percent recycled aluminum in the enclosure and 100 percent recycled cobalt in the battery. iPad mini is manufactured with 40 percent renewable energy, like wind and solar, across the supply chain. It is designed to be durable and repairable, and meets Apple’s high standards for energy efficiency and safe chemistry. As with all Apple products, its paper packaging is 100 percent fiber-based10 and designed to be recycled.
Pricing and Availability
Customers can pre-order iPad mini with A20 Pro starting Wednesday, October 28, at apple.com and in the Apple Store app in 36 countries and regions, including the U.S. It will begin arriving to customers, and will be in Apple Store locations and Apple Authorized Resellers, starting Friday, November 6.
iPad mini will be available in midnight and starlight with 128GB, 256GB, and 512GB configurations.
iPad mini starts at $699 (U.S.) or $58.25 (U.S.) per month for 12 months for the Wi-Fi model, and $849 (U.S.) or $70.75 (U.S.) per month for 12 months for the Wi-Fi + Cellular model.11
Apple Upgrade leasing prices for the iPad mini start at $14.99 (U.S.) per month for a 36-month lease for the Wi-Fi model, and $18.21 (U.S.) per month for a 36-month lease for the Wi-Fi + Cellular model.12
With education savings, iPad mini starts at $649 (U.S.) or $54.08 (U.S.) per month for 12 months.11
The new TechWoven Smart Folio is available in navy blue and taupe, and is available for $79 (U.S.).
Apple Pencil Pro and Apple Pencil (USB-C) are compatible with the new iPad mini. Apple Pencil Pro is available for $129 (U.S.) and $119 (U.S.) with education savings. Apple Pencil (USB-C) is available for $79 (U.S.) and $69 (U.S.) with education savings.
AppleCare delivers exceptional service and support, with flexible options for Apple users. Customers can choose AppleCare+ to cover their new iPad or, in available markets, AppleCare One to protect multiple products in one simple plan. Both plans include coverage for accidents like drops and spills, theft and loss protection on eligible products, battery replacement service, and priority support from Apple Experts. In the U.S., customers can also choose AppleCare One Family, which extends that same coverage to every eligible device across an Apple Family Sharing group for one fixed monthly price. For more information, visit apple.com/applecare.
Apple offers great ways to save on the latest iPad. Customers can trade in their current iPad and get credit toward a new one by visiting the Apple Store online, the Apple Store app, or an Apple Store location. To see what their device is worth, and for terms and conditions, customers can visit apple.com/shop/trade-in.13
Customers in the U.S. who shop at Apple using Apple Card14 can pay monthly at 0 percent APR when they choose to check out with Apple Card Monthly Installments,15 and they’ll get 3 percent Daily Cash back — all up front. More information — including details on eligibility, exclusions, and Apple Card terms — is available at apple.com/apple-card/monthly-installments.
Customers in the U.S. can also pay for their Wi-Fi + Cellular iPad mini over time when they choose to finance with a carrier.

title: GitHub - DilawarShafiq/nietzschian-debugger: The anti-AI debugger. What doesn't kill your code makes it stronger. Confrontational questioning for developers. · GitHub
content:
Nietzschian Debugger
"What doesn't kill your code makes it stronger."
The anti-AI. Every other tool gives you answers. Nietzschian Debugger confronts you with questions.
You paste your bug. It doesn't fix it. Instead, it:
Challenges your assumptions about what's happening
Forces you to confront the evidence you're avoiding
Tears apart your weak reasoning until only truth remains
Guides you to the "aha!" moment — YOUR moment, not the AI's
Why?
AI is making developers weaker. Copy-paste from ChatGPT, ship, repeat. Nobody understands their own code anymore. Nietzschian Debugger forges stronger developers — through struggle, not shortcuts.
"He who has a why to debug can bear almost any how."
Installation
# Published release (npm, v0.1.0)
npx nietzschian-debugger

# Current source (Python 3.10+)
pip install git+https://github.com/DilawarShafiq/nietzschian-debugger.git
nietzschian debug "your bug"
Requirements:
Node.js >= 20 for the npm release, or Python >= 3.10 for the current source
An Anthropic API key (BYOK — bring your own key)
Setup
Set your Anthropic API key:
# Linux / macOS
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."

# Windows (PowerShell)
$env:ANTHROPIC_API_KEY = "sk-ant-..."

# Windows (CMD)
set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...
Quick Start
# Start a debugging session (default: nietzsche intensity)
nietzschian debug "My API returns 500 but only on Tuesdays"

# Gentle mode — for when you need guidance, not punishment
nietzschian debug --intensity socrates "My login endpoint fails randomly"

# Maximum intensity — for seniors who want pain
nietzschian debug --intensity zarathustra "Memory leak in production"

# Point it at specific code
nietzschian debug "Auth fails in ./src/middleware/auth.ts"
Three Intensity Levels
Level Style Best For
socrates Warm, guiding, scaffolded questions Juniors, learning fundamentals
nietzsche Direct, confrontational, no hand-holding Daily debugging (default)
zarathustra Brutal, adversarial, hostile to weak reasoning Seniors who want real pain
How a Session Looks
  Nietzschian Debugger v0.1.0 — intensity: nietzsche

You: My login endpoint returns 403 for some users

Nietzschian: You say "some users." That's vague. What separates
             the ones who fail from the ones who don't?

You: I'm not sure, it seems random

Nietzschian: "Random" is the word we use when we haven't looked
             hard enough. What do the server logs say for the 403
             responses? Go look. I'll wait.

You: Let me check... oh, they all have expired JWT tokens

Nietzschian: Now we're getting somewhere. Why would some users
             have expired tokens while others don't? What changed
             recently in your auth system?

You: ... oh. We changed the token TTL last week and didn't
     invalidate existing sessions.

Nietzschian: There it is. You didn't need me to tell you — you
             needed to be forced to look.

Session Complete — 4 questions to root cause (Solved)

Your Debugging Profile:
┣ Assumption-checking    ██████████  strong
┣ Evidence-gathering     ██████░░░░  moderate
┗ Root cause speed       ████████░░  strong

"Man is something that shall be overcome."
 — Friedrich Nietzsche
Session Commands
Command Effect
solved or found it End session — you found the root cause
I give up Get one lifeline question, then exit
exit or quit Abandon session immediately
Ctrl+C / Ctrl+D Force quit
Features
Never Gives Answers — Every response is a question. The tool will NEVER tell you the fix.
Real Code Reading — Reference a file path and it reads YOUR actual code, not generic examples.
Contextual Philosophy — Nietzsche when you're avoiding, Seneca when overwhelmed, Sun Tzu when you need strategy.
Growth Score — Track your debugging skills across sessions with visual bar charts.
Session History — All sessions saved locally in .nietzschian/sessions/ for trend tracking.
Sliding Context — Long sessions don't crash; older turns are transparently summarized.
The Philosophy
Traditional AI Nietzschian Debugger
"Here's the fix" "What have you tried?"
Makes you dependent Makes you dangerous
You learn nothing You learn everything
Fast but shallow Painful but permanent
AI gets smarter YOU get smarter
Who Is This For?
Junior developers who want to actually learn, not just copy-paste
Senior developers who miss the struggle that made them good
Engineering managers who want their team thinking, not just prompting
Bootcamp students building real debugging intuition
Anyone who believes the best developer is a self-reliant one
Development
# Clone and install
git clone https://github.com/DilawarShafiq/nietzschian-debugger.git
cd nietzschian-debugger
pip install -e ".[dev]"

# Run tests (121 tests)
pytest

# Run the CLI locally
nietzschian debug "test problem"
Tech Stack
Python >= 3.10
Claude API via the Anthropic SDK
Click for the CLI, Rich for the terminal UI
pytest for testing
License
MIT

title: The Man from the Future: Why Johnny Can't Stop Abstracting
content:
The Man from the Future: Why Johnny Can't Stop Abstracting
- October 26, 2026
I have come to suspect that to most people thinking is painful. Some of us are addicted to thinking. Some of us find it a necessity. Johnny enjoyed it. I even have the suspicion that he enjoyed almost nothing else.
-- Edward Teller, eulogizing John von Neumann
I listened to Ananyo Bhattacharya's "The Man from the Future: The Visionary Life of John von Neumann" in my car during the many commute hours Bay Area traffic afforded me. I thought I should share the Johnny phenomena here.
I knew about von Neumann being a very influential mathematician/scientist/engineer but the full list still left me bedazzled. In his 53 years of life (1903-1957), von Neumann seeded so many fields. Every time there was an important discovery in physics, mathematics or computation, John von Neumann was there. Set theory and the foundations of mathematics. The mathematical formulation of quantum mechanics. Operator algebras (still called von Neumann algebras). Ergodic theory. Game theory. Expected utility theory (which is the foundation of most of modern mathematical economics). The Monte Carlo method. The stored-program computer architecture that every machine you have ever touched is built on. Numerical weather prediction. Fault-tolerant computing. Self-reproducing automata (cellular automata), and arguably, the logical structure of molecular biology, four years before Watson and Crick. There is also, unfortunately, the implosion lens for the Nagasaki bomb, and a decade of hawkish nuclear strategy.

Early years
At six, Janos (the OG hungarian name for Johnny) could divide eight-digit numbers in his head and hold a conversation in ancient Greek. He later added Latin, French, German, English, and Yiddish.  The rumor was that he remembered everything he ever read. Many years later Herman Goldstine decided to test this by asking him to recite "A Tale of Two Cities." Von Neumann started on chapter one and had to be asked to stop fifteen minutes later.
Budapest around 1900 produced an absurd cluster of minds: von Neumann, Eugene Wigner, Edward Teller, Leo Szilard, Paul Erdős, Theodore von Kármán, George Pólya. When several of them turned up at Los Alamos and realized they had gone to high school together, Szilard joked that Hungary was a cover story for a Martian landing. But even inside the Martian cluster, von Neumann was the outlier. Wigner, a Nobel laureate himself, was asked at Los Alamos to explain the Hungarian phenomenon and said there is only one phenomenon that is worthy of explanation, and that phenomenon is John von Neumann. The cluster may be less mysterious than it looks: Budapest was one of the few genuinely welcoming places in Europe for Jewish families, and it pushed them toward the professions the nobility considered beneath them, mathematics among them. The schools then did the rest, with a nationwide math competition and top quality high school teachers.
As for the Johnny phenomenon, from the pedagogical perspective, the following stood out to me from Johnny's early years. The first is the dinner table. Von Neumann's father Miksa (Max), a lawyer turned banker so successful that the Emperor ennobled him for service to the national economy, ran the evening meal as a seminar. He would start by going through his own day: the cases he argued, the deals he negotiated, whatever was on his mind. Then each of the three boys would present on what they had been reading. The whole family would then argue about Heine's poetry, or antisemitism in Europe, or the paradoxes of omnipotence. Sometimes Max would bring home business clients, and the boys were allowed to grill them about whatever they wanted funded. Frequent guests included the director of Budapest's Theoretical Physics Institute and one of Freud's students.
The second is the languages. Max knew the good times could end, told his sons so explicitly, and wanted them able to survive anywhere in any language. He was preparing them to flee. He was right. When John was fifteen, the communists took over Hungary and targeted rich families like his. A few months later the counterrevolutionaries beat the communists and then massacred thousands of Jews for supposedly collaborating. The von Neumanns survived by leaving the country at the right moments, and possibly by being too rich.
Johnny's first ten years included no formal schooling at all, because organized primary schools were not a tradition there yet. He had governesses, private teachers, and his father's enormous library, and he apparently used it to memorize a 44-volume German history of the world, which he would later deploy to freak people out at parties.
Finally, when he did get to the Fasori Gymnasium at eleven, the math teacher, László Rátz, concluded fairly quickly that he could not teach this kid and arranged a private tutor. The tutor was Gábor Szegő, who went on to chair the math department at Stanford. Szegő is said to have come away from the first lessons in tears at what the boy could already do. The results of this tutelage showed up a couple years later. At seventeen Johnny gave a new definition of the ordinal numbers, where each number simply is the set of all the numbers before it. Zero is the empty set. One is the set containing zero. Two is the set containing zero and one. And so on up into the infinite ordinals, with nothing but the empty set and a pair of braces to build from. If you think about it, this is a very computer-science-y way to define numbers: an inductive datatype with one constructor. 
He pushed this further in his doctoral thesis a few years later. Set theory at the time was still suffering from the paradoxes, Russell's set of all sets that do not contain themselves being the famous one. Johnny's fix was essentially a type system for sets: the ordinary ones you can put inside other sets, and the oversized ones you can talk about but never use as an element. The paradox then becomes a type error. Note that it is the same abstraction move in both times: take an object everyone thinks they understand, and replace it with the smallest thing that behaves the same way.
Johnny kept doing the same thing in field after field for the next thirty years: arrive, find the smallest set of objects and axioms the mess is actually about, write them down so that everyone can finally argue about the right thing, and then leave before the theorems fell out. Teller said Johnny enjoyed thinking, but I think the addiction was much more specialized than that. His real superpower was "the art of abstraction".
Look at the list from the introduction again with this in mind. Matrix mechanics and wave mechanics looked like rival theories until he noticed they were two coordinate systems on the same Hilbert space. Economists thought comparing preferences across people was hopeless until he asked what minimal consistency axioms a chooser has to satisfy, and derived a cardinal utility scale from them in an afternoon. Self-reproduction looked like it needed an infinite recursion of blueprints until he separated "read the tape as instructions" from "copy the tape as data."

Making quantum mechanics rigorous
Having finished his PhD at 21, Johnny arrived at Göttingen at 22 because it was the world capital of mathematics, under Hilbert. The timing couldn't have been better. Heisenberg, one year older, was down the hall having just invented matrix mechanics. A year later Schrödinger produced wave mechanics in Vienna. The two gave the same answers and implied completely different pictures of reality, and physicists were uneasy with both: matrices were unfamiliar mathematics then, and nobody could say what the waves were. Von Neumann's first move was to prove the two were the same theory in different forms. Then he wrote "Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics" (1932), which set the whole thing up rigorously in Hilbert space. The author of the book Bhattacharya, who did physics as an undergrad, points out that this is still the most watertight formulation we have. 
Once the math was clean, the measurement problem became more visible. Where does the wave function actually collapse? At the apparatus, the detector, the retina, or the conscious observer? Von Neumann declined to take a position, but proved it does not matter mathematically where you draw the line because the answer comes out the same. That line is now called the von Neumann cut.

Game theory and economics
Nothing much came of game theory until von Neumann proved the minimax theorem in 1928, in his early twenties. Every two-player zero-sum game has a solution: either a strategy one player can pursue to win, or a mixed strategy with randomness in it (e.g., rock-paper-scissors). Then he lost interest and wandered off, as was his habit.
He came back when Oskar Morgenstern turned up at Princeton. Morgenstern, an economist, was stuck on what is essentially a liveness bug in economic modeling: you intervene in an economy, people adjust their behavior in response, which invalidates the model you used to design the intervention, so you build a new model, which they also adjust to. An infinite loop. Morgenstern had concluded that all attempts to model economies must fail, which made him unpopular right up until the Wall Street crash made him look prescient. Von Neumann had the tools to attack the problem. Over about eighteen months they produced the 600-page "Theory of Games and Economic Behavior" (1944) and founded the field. Johnny did this as a hobby. During those same years he was designing implosion lenses at Los Alamos and building the first programmable computers. He would drop in on Morgenstern for a long session and then vanish back into the rest of his life.
Two things from this work are still everywhere. The first is the axiomatization of expected utility. Putting human preferences on a cardinal scale and comparing them across people was considered more or less impossible, and von Neumann sat down one afternoon and did it. This relates uncomfortably with the longtermism material from the Cal Newport/Émile Torres conversation I wrote up recently. Expected value math is a hell of a drug.
The second is its limited model. His framework is built on zero-sum games and on coalitions: given n players, which coalitions are stable? Most of his book is about that, but a lot of the world is not zero-sum. Nash's non-cooperative equilibrium, which generalizes minimax, is what opened that up, and von Neumann rejected it essentially out of hand when Nash walked into his office. To him it was a trivial step, a fixed-point argument he could see through instantly. He misjudged the importance of the non-cooperative approach. Bhattacharya flags a nice irony here: von Neumann, the alleged Cold War hawk and the model for Dr. Strangelove, built a theory centered on people talking to each other and forming working coalitions. It was Nash, who had trouble with people, who formalized everyone optimizing alone. All models are wrong, but some are useful.

The computer
In 1944 Johnny ran into Herman Goldstine on a train platform at Aberdeen, found out about the ENIAC, and attached himself to the project. In 1945 he wrote the "First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC", laying out the stored-program architecture: one memory holding both instructions and data, a control unit, an arithmetic unit, I/O. That is now the architecture of virtually all computers, from the desktops to smartphones, eighty years later.
Von Neumann was adamant that the technical details go into the public domain, and circulating that draft is exactly what made the architecture unpatentable. So Johnny was also an early proponent of Open Source. He did the same with the IAS machine design, which got copied worldwide and produced a run of machines with goofy names: MANIAC at Los Alamos, JOHNNIAC at RAND, ILLIAC at Illinois, SILLIAC in Sydney, WEIZAC in Israel. For a man who gets painted as the cold rationalist hawk, putting the foundational design of the computing industry into the commons on purpose is a generous act.
He also, with Ulam, invented the Monte Carlo method, then needed random numbers for it and had to invent pseudorandom generation. And he put the first serious application on these machines himself. The IAS Meteorology Project ran the first computerized weather forecast in 1950. Numerical weather prediction, and by extension climate modeling, is a von Neumann production.

Reliable organisms from unreliable components
In 1952 von Neumann gave a lecture series at Caltech titled "Probabilistic Logics and the Synthesis of Reliable Organisms from Unreliable Components." The vacuum tubes of the day failed constantly, and the standard engineering response was to make better tubes. His response was to ask whether you could build an arbitrarily reliable machine out of components that are guaranteed to fail, using redundancy and majority voting, and then to work out how much redundancy you actually need. That is one of the founding ideas of fault-tolerant computing, and gives rise to replicated state machine, quorums, and Paxos.

Self-reproducing automata
In the late 1940s, Johnny started asking what it would take for a machine to build a copy of itself. The naive worry is infinite recursion: the machine needs a blueprint of itself, and that blueprint must include a blueprint of the blueprint, and so on down forever. His solution (worked out with Ulam's suggestion to set it in a discrete cellular framework) was to split the role of the description. You have a universal constructor plus a tape describing it. The constructor reads the tape as "instructions" and builds the described machine. Then it copies the tape as uninterpreted "data" and attaches the copy to the offspring. One description is used twice in two completely different modes. This is the stored-program idea again, three years after EDVAC: the same bits are instructions when you execute them and data when you copy them.
He published this in 1948 and 1949. Watson and Crick published the structure of DNA in 1953. So von Neumann derived, from pure logic, the necessary architecture of biological reproduction. That there must be a stored description. That it must be read in two distinct ways. That this separation is precisely what makes open-ended evolution possible. Translation and transcription. Genotype and phenotype. He got the shape of the answer years before anyone knew what the molecule was.
The 29-state cellular automaton he built to prove it was also, incidentally, the first cellular automaton. Conway's Game of Life, Wolfram's entire research program, artificial life, and a foundations of what people now call synthetic biology all descend from his formal model. "Theory of Self-Reproducing Automata" was published posthumously in 1966.
His last work, also published posthumously, was "The Computer and the Brain" (1958). In it he observes that the brain achieves what it does with terribl

title: Virtual and Real World Combine at LAN Party - Los Angeles Times

By P.J. HUFFSTUTTER
Aug. 10, 1998 12 AM PT
TIMES STAFF WRITER
It is a rave unlike any other.
The moon hangs warm and fat in Costa Mesa, casting its midsummer light across the roof of a corporate office complex. Inside, Andrea Bruns squeezes through the sweaty chaos, edging past a couple grinding on the impromptu dance floor and the rows of men playing computer games. Flashing strobes and the glow of dozens of monitors cast psychedelic patterns of light across her pale face.
Every month, Bruns grabs her computer out of her San Rafael apartment, crams it into her tiny black convertible and heads for Southern California. Her destination is the BeatDown, a monthly computer-game party that has hundreds of fans vying for an invitation. The protocol is simple: Bring cash, a personal computer and the desire to revel for up to 72 hours straight.

Guide on how to grow chocolate at home
by CocoTerra | Jan 15, 2024 | Chocolate Information
Follow CocoTerra on Social Media
FollowFollowFollowFollow
Growing chocolate at home might sound like a wild idea, right? Chocolate originates from cacao trees, which demand a tropical climate, specific growing conditions, and several years to reach maturity in order to flower and fruit to produce cacao pods. However, our CocoTerra founder, Nate Saal, took on the challenge and grew cacao trees in Northern California to test the limits of growing cacao. Surprisingly, he succeeded!
Keep reading to discover how you can grow a cacao tree in your home and make your own chocolate.
What is needed to grow chocolate at home?
To grow chocolate, you’ll need a few essential items:
Cacao seeds or seedlings
A series of small to large pots
A tropical/subtropical climate or a warm indoor space (an outdoor greenhouse can also work)
A window or skylight with filtered sunlight
Water
Soil and fertilizer
Should I grow my chocolate indoors or outdoors?
Deciding whether to grow your chocolate indoors or outdoors depends on where you live and what temperatures the tree will be exposed to in your particular environment. Cacao trees usually do well in warm and humid tropical climates, so if you’re in such an area, growing them outside is a good choice. Cacao trees are also susceptible to wind damage, so make sure they are not too exposed.  However, if you’re in a colder region, it might be better to grow your cacao trees indoors to give them the warmth they require.  In the San Francisco Bay Area, indoors is the only option since it can drop to near freezing during the winter months.
Keep in mind that growing cacao at home might be a bit harder since the tree is  not in its usual environment. But if you’re dedicated and create the right conditions, you can enjoy the satisfying experience of growing your own chocolate ingredients.
Cacao seeds guide – Types and which one to choose
Selecting the perfect cacao type is essential for your chocolate-making adventure. In this article 10 distinct varieties of cacao: Ultimate cacao guide, we explore different varieties of cacao from around the world. Each variety has its own unique flavor profile, ranging from fruity and floral to nutty and fudgy.  When making your selection, make sure that you check the status of your selected variety to determine if it is self fertile or not.  If not, you will have to grow at least two trees in order to cross-pollinate the flowers.
We also strongly recommend the book “The New Taste of Chocolate, Revised,” which delves into genetic discoveries related to chocolate varieties.
Step by step Guide on how to grow chocolate at home
Step 1 – Location Selection
Cacao trees love tropical climates with steady warmth and humidity, usually within 20 degrees of the equator. If you’re thinking about growing your chocolate at home, it’s important to consider your local climate. Depending on where you live, you might decide whether to grow your cacao indoors or outdoors. Temperatures between 65-85 F are ideal for cacao trees. Anything colder and it will die. Additionally, keep in mind that cacao trees can thrive in both full sun and partial shade, but seedlings shouldn’t be exposed to intense sunlight. If you’re growing your cacao plant indoors, a sunny window is an ideal spot for it.
Step 2 – Prepping the Seeds
First and foremost, get cacao seeds from a reliable source and make sure they are fresh.  If the seeds are fresh, they will be covered in a white pulp.  Wash off all the pulp by lightly rubbing the outside of the seeds under running water.  You can carefully peel off the outer seed shell, which will assist the germination (not easy to do and will take some practice).  Once the seeds are prepped, place them in a bowl of water for 1-2 days until the root starts to poke out the side of the seed.  Your seeds are now ready to plant.  Don’t leave them in the water for too long or they might start to rot.
Step 3 – Planting the Seeds
Plant the seeds in small pots filled with soil that drains well and is rich in nutrients. Ideally, the soil contains about 50% perlite or coarse sand to ensure proper drainage.  When planting the seeds, make sure that they are pointing root side down and only bury them halfway into the soil.  The seeds are prone to rotting, so make sure they are poking out of the soil.
Step 4 – Germination
Ensure the soil stays consistently moist and warm to support germination, which might take several weeks.  Cacao trees prefer consistent soil moisture, so regular watering is key to their well-being.  Watering twice a week should be sufficient. The seed will slowly elevate themselves as the root pushes into the soil and it will open to reveal a few true leaves.  
Step 5 – Transplanting Seedlings 
Once seedlings have several leaves, transplant them to larger containers with well-draining soil.  Cacao trees prefer slightly acidic soil. Provide regular, deep watering, especially during dry periods. From time to time, your cacao tree will surge in growth and you will notice your plant quickly doubling in size.   Misting your trees with water or keeping an open water container near them to increase humidity will make your plants happy.
If your climate allows, consider planting the cacao tree outdoors in a location with partial shade.
Step 6 – Repotting
Each year, your tree should grow several feet in height.  As the trunk gets bigger and bigger and the tree gets taller and taller, transplant your cacao tree to larger and larger pots.  Eventually, if you are keeping your cacao tree potted, you’ll want to transplant it to a pot that is 20 inches or larger in diameter.
Step 6 –  Tree Maturation
When the tree hits about 5-7 ft and still a single trunk structure, it will naturally send out perpendicular branches that run almost parallel to the ground.   There is no need to prune or “top” the cacao plant as it will naturally transform its structure and develop a canopy.
As your tree continues to mature, it will start to produce your first little cacao flower buds!
Step 7 –  Hand-pollination
There are no birds or bees indoors, so your flowers will have to be hand-pollinated (of course, if you’ve been read the CocoTerra blog, you know that only midges pollinate cacao flowers, so even if your plant were outdoors, you would still need to hand pollinate).
Hand-pollinating cocoa flowers involves transferring pollen from the male parts (stamen) to the female parts (pistil) to facilitate fertilization. Begin by selecting recently opened flowers. Gently tap a mature male flower to release pollen onto a clean, dry surface. Collect the pollen using a fine brush or cotton swab. To improve the likelihood of successful fertilization, repeat the hand-pollination process on several female flowers.  Alternatively, you can pluck the stamen off one flower with a forceps and gently touch it to the pistil of another flower.  The flowers are only fertile for a day or two, so don’t miss your opportunity to pollinate.  Also, the flowers are more receptive in the early morning hours, so as they say… the early bird gets the cacao pod!
Step 8 –  The first sign of success!  
The initial sign of success! A baby cacao fruit emerges… At this stage, witnessing the formation of a tiny pod indicates that the most challenging phase has passed, and you are on the right path!  Yes, this is an exciting time, but (there’s always a “but”), cacao trees have a habit of aborting fruit if conditions are not right.  This process is called cherelle wilt and it is a natural fruit-thinning process where the baby pods will dry out after 6-8 weeks.  Don’t be discouraged.  Keep hand pollinating and eventually, your fruit will make it past this critical stage.
Step 9 –  Patience and Care
Be patient and continue to care for the tree, The cacao pods will gradually increase in size, growing a little each day.
Step 10 –  Ripening
The pod will begin to plump up, and its color will transition from green to a yellowish tone (the color will depend on the particular variety that you are growing). 
When the pod has a yellow tone this is an indication that the cocoa beans inside are maturing. Ripe cocoa pods tend to become slightly softer compared to their firmer, unripe pods.
Step 11 –  Harvesting 
With a lot of patience and hard work now you will have a fresh cacao pod ready to be transformed into delicious chocolate.   Of course you know that this is just the start of the chocolate-making process.  
Carefully use a sharp knife to cut the stem of the mature pod, ensuring not to harm the surrounding tree or other pods. Extract the fresh seeds and pulp.  You can suck on the seeds and enjoy the tropical tasting pulp, or you can collect them all together and ferment them to initiate the chocolate-making process for your own delicious homemade, single-origin chocolate bar.
Voila! That’s how our founder, Nate Saal was able to make a single-origin cacao from California!

title: Migrate Your 300-Node Redis Cluster to Just 3 Lavik Nodes · Lavik
content:
Lavik
/
blog
Migrate Your 300-Node Redis Cluster to Just 3 Lavik Nodes
Why keep buying servers for RAM? Lavik combines NVMe SSD capacity with throughput above Redis on DRAM. Explore the architecture, benchmarks and economics of a 300-to-3 consolidation.
Lavik project · 2026-10-15
Architecture
Use Case
Benchmark
IN THIS ARTICLE
1. Agents need more state—and fast access to it
2. Stop adding servers just to add memory
3. Build capacity around NVMe SSD
4. Faster than Redis on DRAM—with values on SSD
5. Fewer nodes mean less cluster machinery
6. Move the workload, keep the service requirements
7. Give agent state room to grow
Benchmark and sizing notes
Memory is full. CPU still has room. Yet the next increase in retained data means another Redis shard, another replica, and another pair of servers to operate. For a capacity-bound application, that is an expensive way to grow. Lavik changes the resource that determines capacity: application values live on NVMe SSD, served by an engine that measured 1.14 million GETs per second—faster than Redis on DRAM in the published comparison. That combination opens a much more attractive design: consolidate a memory-bound fleet onto a few storage-dense hosts, with room for the next generation of agent state.
[13]
[1]
Capacity model: 300 E2s_v4 Redis VMs versus two L16as_v4 Lavik data VMs and one E2s_v4 Meta-only voter. One Meta member runs on each VM; only the primary and follower hold the dataset.
[1]
[28]
[29]
1. Agents need more state—and fast access to it
A human-facing application might retain a profile, a session and a set of features per user. An agent application can retain all of these for a research assistant, a coding assistant and multiple background workers acting on that user’s behalf. Each agent accumulates execution state, observations and working context. An agent that runs occasionally may still need its state immediately when it resumes. Capacity grows with the number of agents, the size of their state and how long it remains useful; request volume does not have to grow at the same rate.
[1]
At one billion agents, just 1 KB of features each produces approximately 1 TB of values. Increase that to 10 KB and the dataset reaches 10 TB; at 100 KB, it reaches 100 TB, before keys, indexes or replication. Applications still need low-latency reads and updates through familiar Redis clients and data structures. Keeping every retained value in expensive DRAM makes that combination harder to afford. Lavik is designed to make NVMe SSD capacity practical for those latency-sensitive workloads.
[1]
[6]
Value payload for one billion retained agents · decimal units
Bytes per agent Unique value payload Two copies, values only
1 KB 1 TB 2 TB
10 KB 10 TB 20 TB
100 KB 100 TB 200 TB
Sources and calculation inputs
[1]
2. Stop adding servers just to add memory
Consider 300 Standard_E2s_v4 Azure VMs, each with two vCPUs, 16 GiB RAM and no local SSD, arranged as 150 primaries and 150 replicas. The fleet buys 600 vCPUs and 4,800 GiB of RAM, with 2,400 GiB on the primary side. When memory fills first, expanding this fleet buys additional CPU, networking and operating systems largely to obtain more RAM. The application may need more retained profiles or longer session lifetimes without needing proportionally more compute. This is the central opportunity for Redis cost optimization: choose storage density independently of the processors needed to serve traffic.
[1]
[28]
Use the same Azure region and purchasing model for both deployments: East US 2, Linux pay-as-you-go, in US dollars. Microsoft’s retail rate is $0.126 per hour for Standard_E2s_v4 and $1.376 per hour for Standard_L16as_v4. At 730 hours per month, 300 Redis VMs cost $27,594. Lavik uses two L16as_v4 data VMs and one smaller E2s_v4 voter, totaling $2,100.94 per month. Each data VM includes 16 vCPUs, 128 GiB RAM and 3.84 TB of local NVMe SSD; the voter needs no local SSD or dataset copy.
[27]
[28]
[29]
[1]
Adding flash does not automatically solve the latency problem. Redis describes Flex’s flash access in milliseconds and advises against broad access patterns, large working sets and frequent movement between RAM and flash. For an application with a sub-millisecond latency budget, a millisecond flash path is too slow. Agent workloads that repeatedly revisit different profiles and contexts make this distinction consequential: the storage engine needs to serve a large dataset efficiently even when accesses spread beyond RAM.
[25]
[26]
The monthly VM bill falls by $25,493.06—92.4%—and the annualized saving is $305,916.72. Lavik’s three VMs provide 34 vCPUs and 272 GiB RAM across the deployment, with the two NVMe-equipped nodes handling data and the smaller VM completing the failover quorum. Redis’s 300 VMs provide 600 vCPUs, much of which a memory-bound workload may not need. Storage density reduces the serving fleet, while separating the voter’s role avoids paying for an extra data-sized machine. The table prices self-hosted VMs for both systems; OS disks, backups and traffic are additional deployment costs.
[1]
[27]
[11]
[6]
Azure East US 2 · Linux pay-as-you-go · USD · 730 hours/month. VM-hour rates identify each SKU; monthly and annual costs cover the complete deployment.
Deployment USD / VM-hour Monthly USD Annual USD USD / million operations at 1M average QPS
Redis · 300 × Standard_E2s_v4 $0.126 $27,594.00 $331,128.00 $0.01050
Lavik · 2 × L16as_v4 + 1 × E2s_v4 $1.376 (L16as_v4); $0.126 (E2s_v4) $2,100.94 $25,211.28 $0.00080
Sources and calculation inputs
[27]
[1]
3. Build capacity around NVMe SSD
Build the Lavik deployment from two Standard_L16as_v4 VMs and one Standard_E2s_v4 VM. The primary and follower each have 16 vCPUs, 128 GiB RAM and four 960 GB local NVMe devices, totaling 3.84 TB per data VM. Each runs a Data process and a Meta member. The E2s_v4 runs the third Meta member on two vCPUs and 16 GiB RAM, completing the three-member Raft quorum for automatic failover. This voter-only VM stores control-plane metadata, not application data. The topology has two complete dataset copies and three Meta voters.
[1]
[28]
[29]
[6]
[11]
[7]
The primary and follower each hold a full copy, so the single-copy capacity basis remains 3.84 TB. Including the voter VM, the deployment costs $547.12 per TB-month. Redis’s 150 primaries provide 2,400 GiB, or about 2.577 decimal TB, yielding $10,707.88 per TB-month. These are capacity-normalized VM costs before database overhead and operational free-space reserves. If the primary VM fails, the follower and dedicated voter retain a two-of-three Meta majority to coordinate promotion of the eligible follower. The surviving follower holds the remaining data copy; the voter supplies control-plane participation.
[1]
[27]
[11]
[7]
Monthly VM cost per TB of primary capacity, before database overhead and operational headroom. Replica capacity is counted once.
Deployment Single-copy capacity denominator USD / TB-month
Redis · 300 × E2s_v4 2,400 GiB RAM (≈ 2.577 TB) $10,707.88
Lavik · 2 × L16as_v4 + 1 × E2s_v4 3.84 TB NVMe SSD $547.12
Sources and calculation inputs
[1]
[28]
[29]
[27]
Lavik uses DRAM where it has the most value on the request path: the key index, metadata and active buffers. Values use NVMe SSD capacity. This separates growth in value bytes from growth in index memory, which is particularly useful as agent profiles and retained context become larger. Size RAM from the application’s key count and key lengths, together with buffers, hugepages and replication backlog. In the published large-dataset experiment, a billion-key layout fits a 125.8 GiB host while its values occupy about a terabyte.
[9]
[13]
SPDK makes the storage path explicit. Lavik submits NVMe operations through userspace queue pairs and polls for completions, removing the kernel block-I/O submission path and its syscall and wakeup overhead. Asynchronous requests keep storage work in flight while workers make progress on other commands. Polling trades CPU time for prompt completion handling; queue depth, completion batching and CPU placement determine how effectively that time is used. Modern NVMe devices supply the parallel queues and internal concurrency. The engine must deliver enough independent work to exploit them.
[4]
[5]
[13]
Lavik’s Bycorf workers use coroutines, owner-local mutable state and explicit dispatch between workers. While one command waits for storage, other runnable work can proceed. Ownership keeps common operations close to the state they modify and reduces coordination between cores. That matters at a million operations per second: small amounts of scheduling, synchronization or allocation overhead accumulate into substantial CPU demand. Designing execution and storage together lets Lavik use SSD parallelism without turning every I/O into a stalled request-processing thread.
[6]
[8]
[9]
The optimizations extend through the request path. Eligible disk GETs can use an admitted index snapshot on the connection worker, avoiding owner dispatch when the fast path applies. Parsing handles batches of up to 128 commands, and small pipeline replies can coalesce into 64 KiB writes. Per-worker append streams avoid a staging-buffer allocation for every logical slot. Together, these choices reduce coordination, system calls and buffer overhead. The Redis-compatible interface stays familiar to applications; the implementation underneath is built around efficient concurrent storage access.
[8]
[9]
Large objects receive the same attention. Lavik 0.1.0 supports grouped storage for Strings, Hashes, Sets, Lists, Sorted Sets and Streams. Large strings use 8 KiB segments, while collections use independently addressed groups. A focused operation can work on the relevant part instead of rewriting an entire large object. For an agent profile with frequently changing features and much larger retained state, that layout makes the difference between a small update and unnecessary work across the whole record. NVMe performance depends on both how I/O is scheduled and how much data each operation touches.
[10]
Lavik’s request path: coroutine workers, an in-memory key index and asynchronous SPDK I/O keep NVMe storage busy.
[6]
[8]
[9]
[4]
4. Faster than Redis on DRAM—with values on SSD
The direct benchmark compares Lavik 0.1.0 SPDK with Redis 8.10.2 and Valkey 9.1.2 on the same 16-vCPU Azure server. A separate load generator issues uniform random GETs and SETs over private networking, with 1 KiB values and pipeline depth one. Redis and Valkey serve their values from DRAM; Lavik uses its NVMe storage path. The table shows throughput and client-observed latency together, so readers can choose an operating point against their application’s latency budget.
[13]
At 1,280 connections, Lavik delivers 1,145,772 GET QPS and 971,950 SET QPS. GET throughput is 12.5% higher than Redis and 18.1% higher than Valkey; SET throughput is 2.2% higher than Redis. Lavik’s GET P99 at that point is 3.999 ms, compared with Redis’s 4.415 ms. This is the architectural result that makes consolidation worth considering: NVMe-backed capacity can come with higher throughput than an in-memory server, rather than forcing the application to exchange performance for lower storage cost.
[16]
[13]
Same 1,280-connection runs · QPS rounded to whole operations; all latency columns in milliseconds
System / operation QPS Average P50 P95 P99 P99.9
Lavik 0.1.0 SPDK GET 1,145,772 1.117 1.031 1.511 3.999 7.135
Lavik 0.1.0 SPDK SET 971,950 1.317 1.119 2.783 4.479 7.199
Redis 8.10.2 GET 1,018,735 1.256 1.087 2.479 4.415 7.103
Redis 8.10.2 SET 951,053 1.346 1.135 2.943 4.511 7.231
Valkey 9.1.2 GET 970,288 1.319 1.119 2.511 4.415 7.455
Valkey 9.1.2 SET 808,103 1.583 1.455 2.559 4.047 7.199
Sources and calculation inputs
[16]
[17]
[18]
[19]
[20]
[21]
[22]
Latency also depends on how hard a server is driven. At the billion-key operating point with 80 connections, Lavik delivers 385,514 GET QPS at 0.439 ms P99.9. At 640 connections, it reaches more than a million GETs per second. An infrastructure team can use these curves to select the throughput and tail-latency combination it needs. Keeping headroom for bursts is more useful than sizing a production deployment solely from the highest point on a throughput chart.
[13]
The billion-key dataset contains 1.024 TB of raw values—about 7.6 times the server’s RAM—and reaches 1,069,126 GET QPS. Lavik’s performance therefore extends well beyond a memory-sized dataset. The smaller-instance results tell the same capacity story: on two vCPUs and 16 GiB nominal RAM, increasing the dataset from one million to 100 million 1 KiB values changes peak GET throughput from 215,521 to 215,463 QPS. SET retains 95.2% of its smaller-dataset peak. That is valuable for both a compact service and a large agent platform: capacity can grow without demanding a matching increase in serving nodes.
[13]
[14]
GET and SET across 80–1,280 connections. The 10M-key runs use 30-second windows; the 1B-key runs use 60-second windows and distinct client seeds.
[13]
[16]
Agent state also needs updates. In the separate io_uring YCSB experiment, Lavik processes 529,501 operations per second for a 50/50 read/update mix and 577,373 for a 95/5 mix. These are structured-record operations: HGETALL reads and LAVIK.HREPLACE updates against 100 million records with ten 128-byte fields. They show the relevance of Lavik’s design beyond a pure GET workload, including feature records whose contents change as an agent progresses through a task.
[15]
Separate io_uring YCSB experiment · 100M records, 10 × 128 B fields, 256 workers, no replicas
Lavik workload Total QPS READ P99.9 ms UPDATE P99.9 ms
50% HGETALL / 50% HREPLACE 529,501 5.083 2.831
95% HGETALL / 5% HREPLACE 577,373 1.818 1.578
Sources and calculation inputs
[15]
One million operations per second corresponds to 86.4 billion operations per day if sustained. That level of measured serving performance, combined with NVMe storage density, makes a strong case for reevaluating a memory-bound fleet. Start with the actual traffic envelope—command mix, peak demand, bursts and latency target—and allocate compute to that envelope. Let NVMe SSD provide the capacity for everything the application needs to remember.
[1]
[13]
5. Fewer nodes mean less cluster machinery
Memory-driven growth also expands the topology engineers must operate. Redis Cluster distributes 16,384 hash slots and uses a full-mesh cluster bus. Its specification gives each node N−1 outgoing and N−1 incoming bus connections. Across the cluster, that is N(N−1) initiated connections: 89,700 at 300 nodes, 359,400 at 600 and 999,000 at 1,000. These are cluster-bus connections, separate from application traffic. As agent state expands, adding memory through more nodes also increases the size of this coordination fabric.
[2]
The cluster uses gossip, heartbeat probes and failure reports to maintain membership and health. Local failure suspicion must be reconciled with reports from other

SIMD-accelerated computer vision on a $2 microcontroller — shraiwi
content:
SIMD-accelerated computer vision on a $2 microcontroller
I wrote an accelerated FAST feature detector for the ESP32-S3 that leverages its 128-bit SIMD instructions. It achieves roughly double the performance of the reference implementation, and takes around ~6ms to process a QVGA (320x240) frame. You can find the source code here.
For its price, the ESP32-S3 is a powerhouse of a microcontroller. Within its unassuming plastic package lies a dual-core CPU running at a maximum of 240MHz with a slew of peripherals, including WiFi and Bluetooth Low Energy radios. While digging through its technical reference manual I discovered that the chip supports a limited set of SIMD instructions. For silicon that’s cheaper than the average coffee, that’s pretty cool. Let’s see what exciting things we can do with it!
In the process of writing a SIMD-accelerated FAST corner detector, I learned the basics of assembly on the ESP32-S3, worked around its eccentric limitations, and ended up writing my own basic register allocator, basm.
After some more web browsing, I realized that these instructions weren’t exactly secret, but rather relatively unknown. I wanted to experiment with them myself and write more advanced code than what I could find online. As I’ve been really interested in computer vision lately, I decided on writing a SIMD-accelerated implementation of the FAST feature detector for the ESP32-S3.
I started by looking for example code that uses SIMD instructions. At the time of writing, I could only find three sources:
Larry Bank’s blog, where he explores the feature and provides a minimal example
Espressif’s esp-dsp library, used for DSP-esque features (convolutions, FFT, etc.)
Espressif’s esp-dl library, used for on-chip AI acceleration.
After perusing through them, I was relieved to find that assembly on the ESP32-S3 isn’t that bad. I settled on this general structure:
    .section .rodata
 # read-only data here

    .section .text
    .align 4

    .global add
    .type   add,@function
# a simple function that adds two numbers
# int32_t add(int32_t a, int32_t b)
add:
    entry           sp, 48 # sp (stack pointer) is an alias for a1
    
    #define r_a a2
    #define r_b a3

 # code here
    
 add a2, r_a, r_b # a2 = a + b

    retw.n # return, with a2 containing the return value.
From there, I started writing a SIMD-accelerated version of the FAST corner pre-test. Essentially, it samples one pixel in each cardinal direction and checks if there are at least three “extreme” pixels. In this case, an extreme pixel is one whose absolute difference from the center pixel is above a certain threshold.
I decided on a function that would calculate the extrema count of sixteen pixels at a time, since each vector register can store sixteen eight-bit values. This would be achieved by sampling four “chunks” of pixels in each cardinal direction and comparing them to their respective center pixels.
However, this is where I ran into my first limitation- the ISA doesn’t allow for direct misaligned reads. Under the assumption that the center pixel would be aligned, the east and west blocks would be misaligned:
center
east
west
north
south
Thankfully, the chip has an instruction that allows for extracting a slice of two concatenated registers into another one. Using this functionality, I was able to extract the east and west blocks by reading and extracting slices from the two blocks adjacent to the center block.
Okay, so now I have the pixel data. Time to do some comparisons, right? Wrong. Turns out the ESP32-S3’s only implements comparisons for signed eight-bit numbers. This made processing a little more difficult, because all my pixel data was stored as unsigned eight-bit numbers. If you just reinterpreted the unsigned data as signed data, you get some weird results:
>>> np.int8(np.uint8(range(0, 256, 8)))
array([   0,    8,   16,   24,   32,   40,   48,   56,   64,   72,   80,
         88,   96,  104,  112,  120, -128, -120, -112, -104,  -96,  -88,
        -80,  -72,  -64,  -56,  -48,  -40,  -32,  -24,  -16,   -8],
      dtype=int8)
The range [128 255] gets nonlinearly mapped to [-128 -1], breaking all compare operations. To make this work, I needed to shift the range of the values from [0, 255] to [-128 127]. This should’ve been a simple subtraction, but the instruction set got in the way again: on the ESP32-S3, all the SIMD arithmetic operations are saturating, which meant that all pixel values above 127 would end up being clamped at -128 instead of underflowing to their appropriate values. To overcome this problem, I had to somehow subtract 128 from each number in parallel without using the subtraction instruction. This seemed like a daunting task to me at first, but I eventually arrived at a solution.
Let’s assume that x is the minuend. Here is its digits’ place values:
-128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1
Notice anything interesting? Subtraction is the same as addition by -128, so to compute x - 128, we can just “increment” the number by -128 by adding one to x’s most significant digit, whose place value is -128. We can compute this by simply flipping the highest bit of x. Since XORing any bit with one is the same as taking the bitwise NOT, we can selectively flip the highest bit of x by XORing it with the bit mask 0b10000000, which equal to 0x80. Therefore, x - 128 == x ^ 0x80.
Now, whenever unsigned eight-bit values are loaded in, they are XOR’d with 0x80 to convert them an appropriate (linear) range where the arithmetic and comparisons make sense again.
With those two tricks, I was able to circumvent the limitations of the ESP32-S3 and write the SIMD-accelerated FAST corner pre-test. I also wrote a SIMD-accelerated scoring function using a similar set of operations but I won’t be writing about that here.
In the end, I was able to improve the throughput of the FAST feature detector by about 220%, from 5.1MP/s to 11.2MP/s in my testing. This is well within the acceptable range of performance for realtime computer vision tasks, enabling the ESP32-S3 to easily process a 30fps VGA stream. Not bad for $2!
