title: Build Your Own Reasoning Model: A Full Video Course
content:
Discover more from Ahead of AI
Ahead of AI focuses on machine learning and AI research and is read by more than 200,000 researchers and practitioners who want to stay ahead in a rapidly evolving field.
Over 224,000 subscribers
Subscribe
By subscribing, you agree to Substack's Terms of Use, and acknowledge its Information Collection Notice and Privacy Policy.
Already have an account? Sign in
Building Reasoning Models from the Ground Up: A Full Video Course
Eight videos and over 11 hours of coding, covering evaluation, inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation in Python and PyTorch.
SEBASTIAN RASCHKA, PHD
OCT 24, 2026
310
12
34
Share
I have written a lot about reasoning models here over the last two years on Ahead of AI, including a recent article on mechanisms to control reasoning effort levels in contemporary LLMs. Reasoning models are still as relevant as ever. In fact, almost all current-generation LLMs today are reasoning models or offer a reasoning mode.
For those who are interested in how reasoning models work, including inference scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation, I wrote my recent Build Reasoning Model (From Scratch), which implements these from the ground up in PyTorch, which, in my experience, is still the best way to understand and learn how things really work.
Now, in the last few months, I also sat down and recorded accompanying lectures I wanted to share with you. So, below, you will find eight reasoning model-from-scratch coding videos (11 hours of content).
We start with a pre-trained LLM and implement methods to evaluate and improve it in Python and PyTorch. So, if you enjoyed my Coding LLMs from the Ground Up course last year, this is essentially the sequel (but you can also watch it without the prior course as a prerequisite).
I’m currently taking a short break and will be back soon with more exciting LLM research roundups next month. In the meantime, I hope you enjoy coding along!
How LLMs, reasoning models, and agents relate and fit together
As a small side note, and since I often get asked how reasoning models relate to today’s AI agents, here’s a short section on this before getting started with the videos.
A reasoning model is essentially an upgrade from a conventional LLM, that is, adding more post-training via reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (and optionally inference scaling techniques) to make it more capable of solving more challenging problems. Classically, reasoning models are developed for math and code, but the capabilities can generalize to other problem domains as well.
A reasoning model then functions as the engine inside an agent harness, where the agent harness is a software or tooling framework around the LLM/reasoning model to tackle even more challenging problems (bigger coding tasks, travel booking, and all other sorts of personal assistant tasks). The task of the harness is sophisticated context management and giving the LLM access to tools.
Figure 1: An engine analogy for conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agent harnesses. Figure from my Components of a Coding Agent article.
In this analogy depicted in the figure above, the model is the engine, and the agent harness adds the machinery that lets us use it for various things (as an upgrade from a simple chatbot interface). An agent can use either a conventional LLM or a reasoning model, but reasoning models are the more typical choice as they are more capable. (As mentioned above, most current-gen LLMs are reasoning models with variable reasoning effort settings.)
So, the bottom line is that reasoning models, as the “engine,” remain an important part of understanding modern LLM agents.
The resources accompanying these topics shown above are:
The Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) book and videos
The Build A Reasoning Model (From Scratch) book (and videos below)
The Components of a Coding Agent article on Substack
The videos below focus on developing the reasoning model that can power such a system.
Scope and prerequisites
The reasoning-from-scratch videos focus on a small pre-trained Qwen3 model, where we implement the reasoning methods ourselves in Python and PyTorch. Starting with a pre-trained model lets us focus on the interesting part: evaluation, inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation.
Regarding the prerequisites, I recommend being comfortable with Python and PyTorch. I designed the reasoning materials as standalone content, so the previous Build A Large Language Model (From Scratch) content is recommended but not strictly required.
Compute-resource-wise, you can work through the early text-generation and evaluation examples on a CPU. For the later experiments, especially training, a GPU makes the work much more practical. The first video covers the setup and some more recommendations; the repository also includes hardware and environment recommendations.
Figure 2: An overview of the topics being covered.
The companion book
These videos accompany my book, Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch). If you like to read through the explanation in more detail and at your own pace, work through exercises, and so on, I recommend the book as a companion here.
For the most in-depth learning experience, my suggestion is to read a chapter, work through its code alongside the corresponding video, and then try the exercises.
The book is available from Manning and Amazon, and the print edition is in color!
Figure 3: A random excerpt from the Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch) print book.
Thank you to everyone who has picked up a copy or recommended it to a friend. Your support helps me keep creating these materials.
The videos
As a last, quick side note before getting to the main videos below: For a shorter, more conceptual overview, I also recommend my AI Reasoning Models course on LinkedIn Learning (it should be free for 24h when accessing it via the link there, which shouldn’t then require a LinkedIn Premium subscription).
The course is about 90 minutes and explains how reasoning models work, covering the main ideas behind inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation. It’s a good optional preview if you’d like the main ideas without working through the full implementations below.
To get to the main part of this article, here are the eight main lecture videos.
1. Motivation and code setup
The first video starts with an explanation of the relationship between conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agents. Next, the main topic of the video is setting up the coding environment. This includes installing the Python and PyTorch dependencies (with uv), among others. I also discuss hardware choices and common setup issues.
Topics covered
The relationship between conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agent harnesses
On the benefits of learning through code implementations
The scope of this video series
Installing Python dependencies
Choosing hardware and checking CUDA or Apple Silicon support
Using a remote GPU with VS Code and troubleshooting the environment
Watch video 1 · Setup instructions
2. Loading a base model, text generation, and KV caching
Before adding reasoning methods in the upcoming videos, we need a working base model. Instead of training it from scratch, since that would be a whole other book (see Build A Large Language Model (From Scratch)), we start with a pre-trained model.
Here, we load the pre-trained weights of a Qwen3 0.6B model. Then, we implement the text-generation process via a streaming text generator and add KV caching and model compilation to make text generation more efficient.
These implementations give us the baseline and base components we will evaluate and improve in the following videos.
Topics covered
Encoding text as tokens and decoding it back into text
Downloading Qwen3 weights and loading the model on the selected compute device
Going over tensor shapes, logits, and next-token predictions
Implementing greedy decoding and streaming text generation
Handling end-of-sequence tokens and measuring generation speed
Adding a KV cache to reuse attention keys and values
Combining KV caching with torch.compile and comparing hardware performance
Watch video 2 · Chapter 2 code
3. Building a verifier for evaluation and reinforcement learning
In this lecture, we build a math-answer verifier step by step, from answer extraction to normalization and checking mathematical equivalence. We then use it to evaluate the model on MATH-500.
We use this verifier to evaluate the base model’s performance on the MATH-500 evaluation dataset.
However, the verifier also has a second job later in the series: providing the reward signal for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR).
Topics covered
Intro to verifiers and how they fit into LLM evaluation methods (other methods are covered in the book’s appendix)
Reusing answer verification as a reward signal for RLVR (more on that in chapter 6)
The verifier flow, including extracting final answers, normalizing answers and checking mathematical equivalence
Building an answer grader and an evaluation loop for MATH-500
Comparing base and reasoning models on MATH-500
Watch video 3 · Chapter 3 code
4. Inference-time scaling: sampling and self-consistency
Now we explore ways to improve answers while keeping the model weights fixed. But before implementing specific inference-scaling techniques, we first implement methods to generate diverse answers from the same prompt (this is standard practice in proprietary LLM chatbots, such as ChatGPT).
Concretely, we implement temperature scaling, multinomial sampling, and top-p filtering to generate diverse responses. Then we combine multiple responses through self-consistency, using majority voting over their final answers.
We also examine the tradeoff between answer accuracy and the extra computation needed to generate more candidates.
Topics covered
Comparing how additional compute benefits model performance during training and during inference
A gentle intro to inference-scaling through chain-of-thought prompts
Implementing temperature scaling and multinomial sampling to generate diverse answers
Adding top-p filtering to control the quality of the diverse answers
Combining candidate answers through self-consistency, one of the most popular inference scaling techniques
Evaluating MATH-500 accuracy against the cost of additional inference compute
Watch video 4 · Chapter 4 code
5. Inference-time scaling: scoring and self-refinement
Building on the previous video, we implement scoring functions to compare multiple answers generated from the same prompt. We can also use these scoring methods to break ties in self-consistency (covered in the previous lecture).
The scoring methods covered here include computing token and sequence log probabilities (this will also be relevant in the later reinforcement learning chapters). We then implement a self-refinement loop in which the model critiques an answer and attempts a revision.
The evaluation lets us check how useful those additional steps are for our model.
Topics covered
Using scoring functions for comparing multiple answers and breaking ties
Implementing a simple heuristic scorer
Computing token probabilities and sequence likelihoods (also relevant for the following lectures)
Using log probabilities for improved numerical stability
Building a self-refinement loop for generating critiques and revised answers
Evaluating self-refinement on MATH-500
Watch video 5 · Chapter 5 code
6. Reinforcement learning: implementing GRPO for RLVR
In this lecture, we move on to implementing a training technique called Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR). We first implement a simplified version of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), generate groups of responses, score them with our verifier, and use their relative rewards for the model weight updates during training.
Topics covered
Generating reasoning traces and understanding the relationship between answer lengths and problem-solving abilities
Discussion and comparison of two important LLM post-training methods: Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF) and Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR)
Turning verifier scores into rewards and relative advantages
Computing sequence log probabilities and a simplified GRPO loss
Assembling the training loop with logging and checkpoint saves
Evaluating checkpoints and checking training stability and memory needs
Watch video 6 · Chapter 6 code
7. Reinforcement learning: tracking, clipped policy ratios, and KL terms
Now that we implemented the training loop in the previous lecture, we can revisit it and analyze the training runs in more detail.
Concretely, this video adds more training metrics for inspection and analysis, including entropy and advantage statistics, clipped policy ratios, KL loss term values, and formatted rewards.
We then review the training logs and evaluation results to understand what these additions do and whether additions such as clipped policy ratios and KL loss terms are helpful.
Topics covered
Running longer training experiments and interpreting their logs
Tracking advantages and entropy to understand training behavior
Implementing clipping in the policy loss and analyzing its effects
Adding a KL loss term and discussing reward hacking
Understanding limitations of the simplified KL formulation
Implementing format rewards and conditioning them on answer correctness
Comparing checkpoints on MATH-500 and exploring further GRPO research
Watch video 7 · Chapter 7 code
8. Distilling a reasoning model
Finally, we explore another way to train a small reasoning model, that is, learning from answers generated by a stronger (and bigger) teacher model. We discuss different forms of distillation, prepare reasoning data, and implement the supervised training loop.
We finish this lecture and course by evaluating the distilled model on MATH-500 and comparing the results. This rounds out the series with an alternative to developing reasoning capabilities through reinforcement learning.
Topics covered
Comparing the different combination and approaches to distillation, including soft and hard distillation, and on-policy and off-policy distillation
Creating and collecting teacher-generated answers for the MATH dataset (using DeepSeek R1)
Preparing the distillation dataset, including tokenization and training/validation/test splits
Computing answer-token log probabilities and understanding the cross-entropy loss
Implementing supervised training and tracking training and validation losses
Evaluating checkpoints on MATH-500 and comparing distillation results
Watch video 8 · Chapter 8 code
Final words
As you watch these lectures, I encourage you to pause occasionally and try a small experiment of your own if something interesting comes to mind.
For example, feel free to change the sampling settings, inspect a few failed answers, or try variations of dif

title: Oldest GUI application that still runs on Windows 11 · enlyth
content:
Oldest GUI application that still runs on Windows 11
26 October 2026
·
2 min read
#windows
#gui
Early investigation
For a while I’ve been wondering about a silly question, which is, what’s the oldest application with a GUI that will still run on Windows 11 without modifications or emulation.
Given Windows’ excellent backwards compatibility, I expected the answer to be something impressively old.
Sadly, Windows 11 can’t run 16-bit Windows programs by itself, because 64-bit Windows has no NTVDM, so we’re going to have to find something from the early NT era.
I remember asking this question a while ago on an anonymous forum, where someone pointed me to Win32s, and suggested to find an early release version of it with FREECELL.exe.
So I did exactly that, and lo and behold, FREECELL.EXE with a date modified of 22-Feb-93 running and fully playable, without any changes on the latest version of Windows 11:
At the time of this post, that’s a 33 years and 8 months old application, which is impressively almost as old as me.
So I kinda thought “cool”, considered this a solved mystery and forgot about it shortly afterwards. But for some reason, this question popped into my mind again lately and this time I decided to dig deeper to see if I can find something older.
Further efforts
Digging through old Windows versions on the Internet Archive, I found some early NT 3.1 pre-release versions that seemed promising, but the main issue seemed to be either incompatibility with today’s executable format or API changes that came later in development.
The earliest 1991 versions used a draft PE format not compatible with modern Windows, and builds up to mid-1992 assumed the cdecl calling convention instead of stdcall for Windows API calls, so arguments would get removed twice, as such:
push hwnd          ; 4 bytes of args
call [ShowWindow]  ; Win11 ShowWindow is stdcall, ends with "ret 4" and removes them
add  esp, 4        ; the 1992 caller removes them again
Which would understandably cause the program to crash.
There was one application that caught my eye though, from Build 347, and that was CDPLAYER.EXE, linked on 16-Nov-1992. By then the calling convention was fixed, but the other programs in that build crash in their bundled C runtime. CDPLAYER.EXE avoids that by using the system’s crtdll.dll, and Windows 11 still ships a crtdll.dll in SysWOW64.
If you start the program, you get something like this:
That is because, duh, my computer doesn’t have a CD-ROM drive. But you can use a small DLL (cdemu.dll) to emulate one with some fake audio data and actually get it to play audio:
Pretty cool for a program that’s almost 34 years old!
What if we cheat?
So earlier I mentioned that 16-bit programs are out of the picture because they are no longer supported.
But if you want, you can use something like otvdm to run older Windows applications.
Behold, a fully playable version of REVERSI.EXE dated 15-Nov-1985 running on Windows 11, taken from Windows 1.01:
And although using otvdm does feel like cheating, I thought it was cool enough to include in this post.

title: pylance-release/docs/tsp/type-server-protocol.md at main · microsoft/pylance-release · GitHub
content:
Type Server Protocol
The Type Server Protocol (TSP) is a JSON-RPC protocol for asking a type server for Python analysis data. A type server maintains the type-analysis state for a workspace and answers requests for the protocol version, snapshots, Python search paths, import resolution, and type queries (computed, declared, and expected types).
The protocol uses Language Server Protocol (LSP) data shapes and conventions where they are useful, such as Position and Range, and it represents URIs as strings the same way LSP does. TSP methods use the typeServer/ prefix.
The protocol artifacts in this folder are the authoritative definitions:
typeServerProtocol.ts defines the TypeScript interfaces and request types.
tsp.json is the machine-readable protocol model.
tsp.schema.json is the JSON schema for the protocol model.
Version History
TSP uses semantic version strings for client/server compatibility checks. While the protocol is in the 0.x line, minor version changes may be breaking. Patch version changes remain backward compatible within the same minor line.
Version Changes
0.1.0 Initial protocol version.
0.2.0 Added request types and fields.
0.3.0 Switched to more complex type shapes.
0.4.0 Switched to the Type union and stub-based type payloads.
0.4.1 Added multi-connection negotiation and the typeServer/connection control request.
Connection Model
A client starts a type server and communicates with it over the main JSON-RPC connection using a transport the server supports, such as stdio or Node IPC. When using stdio, stdout must be reserved for JSON-RPC protocol messages.
A type server is expected to receive enough workspace and document state to answer the TSP requests it supports. Clients commonly use normal LSP initialization and document synchronization for this state, then send typeServer/* requests on the same JSON-RPC connection.
TSP also supports optional extra read-only connections. The original connection remains the main connection and owns initialization, workspace state, document synchronization, state-changing notifications, and connection control. Extra connections are opened only after client and server negotiate support during initialization.
Startup Sequence
A typical session follows this order:
The client starts or connects to the type server.
The client and server initialize any shared workspace state, commonly through the LSP initialize and initialized messages.
The client calls typeServer/getSupportedProtocolVersion and verifies that the returned semver string is compatible with the protocol version it expects.
The client calls typeServer/getSnapshot to obtain the first snapshot identifier.
The client sends type-query, import-resolution, or search-path requests that include the current snapshot when required by the request shape.
The server sends typeServer/snapshotChanged when prior type results are no longer valid.
Multi-Connection Mode
Multi-connection mode is an optional performance feature. It lets a client open additional local channels to the same type server for read-only TSP requests, while the main connection continues to own the mutable workspace state.
Clients should use multi-connection mode only when they can benefit from concurrent read-only work, such as high-volume type queries or background workers that should not block the main JSON-RPC connection. A server must still work correctly in single-connection mode. Multi-connection support must not be required for protocol correctness.
Capability Handshake
Multi-connection support is negotiated through the normal LSP initialize request and response. A client that can open extra TSP channels advertises the supported transport kinds under capabilities.experimental.typeServerMultiConnection:
{
    "capabilities": {
        "experimental": {
            "typeServerMultiConnection": {
                "supportedTransports": ["ipc"]
            }
        }
    }
}
A server that can serve extra TSP channels returns the same capability shape in the initialize result:
{
    "capabilities": {
        "experimental": {
            "typeServerMultiConnection": {
                "supportedTransports": ["ipc"]
            }
        }
    }
}
Multi-connection mode is enabled only when both sides advertise typeServerMultiConnection and the two supportedTransports lists have at least one transport in common. If either side omits the capability, or if there is no common transport, the session remains single-connection and the client must not send typeServer/connection.
The currently supported built-in transport kind for extra connections is ipc. This negotiation is separate from the main connection, which can use stdio or Node IPC.
Opening An Extra Connection
After initialization and transport negotiation, the client opens an extra channel by sending typeServer/connection on the main connection:
{
    "type": "open",
    "kind": "ipc",
    "args": ["<ipc-endpoint>"]
}
For ipc, the args array identifies the endpoint or endpoints that the server should connect to. The server should validate the request, connect to the supplied endpoint promptly, and return a result with success: true when it accepts the request. If the server cannot open the channel, it should return success: false and include a short message when useful for logs.
IPC Endpoint Arguments
An ipc endpoint is expected to provide a full-duplex JSON-RPC stream when the platform IPC mechanism supports it. In that case, args contains one endpoint string:
{
    "type": "open",
    "kind": "ipc",
    "args": ["<full-duplex-ipc-endpoint>"]
}
If the platform IPC mechanism exposes only one-way endpoints, args contains two endpoint strings. The endpoint names are from the type server's perspective: the first endpoint is the server input stream, and the second endpoint is the server output stream.
{
    "type": "open",
    "kind": "ipc",
    "args": ["<input-ipc-endpoint>", "<output-ipc-endpoint>"]
}
Closing An Extra Connection
The client closes an extra channel by sending typeServer/connection on the main connection with the same transport kind and endpoint identity:
{
    "type": "close",
    "kind": "ipc",
    "args": ["<ipc-endpoint>"]
}
The server should stop serving the matching extra channel and close the transport promptly. A client may also tear down its local transport if the server does not complete the close within the client's timeout budget.
The close request should use the same args shape that opened the channel: one endpoint for a full-duplex IPC stream, or the same input/output endpoint pair for a split IPC stream.
Allowed Traffic
The main connection owns all state-changing traffic. The following must remain main-connection-only:
LSP initialization and lifecycle messages.
Workspace, configuration, file-watcher, and document synchronization notifications.
Server-to-client snapshot notifications.
The typeServer/connection control request.
Extra connections are TSP-only and read-only. They may be used for requests that do not mutate server state and whose results are valid for the snapshot supplied by the client.
The allowed TSP messages on an extra connection are bound to the negotiated TSP version. If a server reports support for a TSP version and advertises multi-connection support for that session, it must support every extra-connection TSP message defined for that version.
The table below lists the TSP version that first allows each message on an extra connection:
TSP version Extra-connection message
0.4.1 typeServer/getSupportedProtocolVersion
0.4.1 typeServer/getSnapshot
0.4.1 typeServer/getPythonSearchPaths
0.4.1 typeServer/resolveImport
0.4.1 typeServer/getComputedType
0.4.1 typeServer/getDeclaredType
0.4.1 typeServer/getExpectedType
Servers should reject LSP traffic, state-changing notifications, typeServer/connection, and any TSP message not allowed for the negotiated TSP version when received on an extra connection.
Snapshots
A snapshot is a non-negative integer that identifies a point-in-time view of the type server's analysis state. Type handles, declarations, symbols, and other returned objects are valid only for the snapshot in which they were returned unless a request explicitly says otherwise.
The type server must advance the snapshot whenever a previously returned type-analysis result may be invalid. Typical invalidating events include opened-file changes, closed files, configuration changes, watched-file changes, dependency changes, or any cache reset that changes analysis results.
Snapshot rules:
typeServer/getSnapshot returns the current snapshot identifier.
Snapshot identifiers must not decrease during a session.
typeServer/snapshotChanged reports the previous and new snapshot identifiers.
Requests that include a stale snapshot should fail with a JSON-RPC error that lets the client retry with a fresh snapshot. LSP's ServerCancelled error code (-32802) is the preferred error for this case.
Positions And Ranges
TSP follows LSP position conventions:
Lines are zero-based.
Character offsets are zero-based UTF-16 code units.
Ranges identify source spans using a start position and end position.
If a type server stores source locations in another encoding, it must convert locations at the protocol boundary. Incorrect conversion can cause the client to request information for the wrong syntax node.
Nodes, Declarations, And Handles
The type-query requests (typeServer/getComputedType, typeServer/getDeclaredType, typeServer/getExpectedType) identify a source construct with an arg that is either a node or a declaration. A node is a URI plus a source range. A declaration describes where and how a symbol is defined and is either a regular declaration, which is backed by a source AST node, or a synthesized declaration, which is created by the type checker and has no source node.
InvalidHandle is -1 and represents an invalid or unavailable handle. Clients and servers should treat it as a sentinel value, not as a valid object identifier.
Type Results
Type results are JSON-serializable tagged objects. Each type includes a discriminator that tells the client how to interpret the rest of the object. The protocol supports built-in types, declared types, functions, classes, unions, modules, type variables, overload sets, synthesized types, and type references.
Every type object carries a numeric kind discriminator, a numeric id, and a bitfield of flags:
kind Type Description
0 BuiltIn unknown, any, unbound, ellipsis, never, and similar
1 Declared Base for source-declared types (rarely used directly)
2 Function Functions and methods from def statements
3 Class Classes and their instances
4 Union Union types (int | str | None)
5 Module Module objects (import os produces a Module type for os)
6 TypeVar Type variables (T, P, Ts)
7 Overloaded Functions with multiple @overload signatures
8 Synthesized Types synthesized by the type checker
9 TypeReference Reference to another type by id, used for deduplication and cycles
Type objects are snapshot-bound, and type IDs are response-local:
A returned type object is valid only for the snapshot used by the request that produced it.
Type IDs are used to connect TypeReference objects to earlier type objects in the same serialized response graph.
Type IDs are not a stable global identity for a snapshot and should not be compared across separate responses.
Type references should be used to avoid duplicating large or recursive type graphs within one response.
Protocol Surface
The current protocol is intentionally small. The exact parameters and result shapes are defined in the protocol artifacts; the table below lists every TSP message with its direction and payload shape.
Message Direction Params Result
typeServer/getSupportedProtocolVersion client → server none string (semver)
typeServer/getSnapshot client → server none number
typeServer/snapshotChanged server → client { old: number, new: number } notification
typeServer/connection client → server { type: "open" | "close", kind, args? } { success, message? }
typeServer/getPythonSearchPaths client → server { fromUri, snapshot } string[] | undefined
typeServer/resolveImport client → server { sourceUri, moduleDescriptor, snapshot } string | undefined
typeServer/getComputedType client → server { arg: Declaration | Node, snapshot } Type | undefined
typeServer/getDeclaredType client → server { arg: Declaration | Node, snapshot } Type | undefined
typeServer/getExpectedType client → server { arg: Declaration | Node, snapshot } Type | undefined
A type server should implement the messages required by the client it integrates with and return undefined only where the protocol's result type allows it.
Type Queries
The three type-query requests differ by which type they report for the same node or declaration:
typeServer/getComputedType returns the type inferred from code flow. After narrowing a to int, the computed type of b in b = a + 1 is int.
typeServer/getDeclaredType returns the type explicitly written in the source. For def foo(a: int | str), the declared type of a is int | str.
typeServer/getExpectedType returns the type the surrounding context expects. For the call foo(4), the expected type of the argument is int | str.
Error Handling
Use standard JSON-RPC error responses.
Situation Error code Guidance
Stale snapshot -32802 (ServerCancelled) The client can request a fresh snapshot and retry.
Invalid parameters -32602 (InvalidParams) Required fields are missing or malformed.
Internal failure -32603 (InternalError) The server failed unexpectedly while handling a valid request.
Errors should include enough message detail for a client log to identify the failed request, but they should not expose local secrets or implementation-only state.
Compatibility Checklist
A compatible type server should verify these behaviors:
typeServer/getSupportedProtocolVersion returns a semver string supported by the client.
All request and notification payloads serialize and deserialize according to the protocol artifacts.
typeServer/getSnapshot returns a non-negative snapshot and snapshots do not go backward.
Document, configuration, and watched-file changes invalidate snapshots when they can change returned analysis data.
Requests with stale snapshots fail with a retryable cancellation error.
Position and range conversions use LSP zero-based UTF-16 conventions.
Import-resolution requests return document URIs or no result according to the protocol result type.
Type queries (computed, declared, and expected) return well-formed Type objects, or undefined, for the snapshot supplied by the client.
Multi-connection support is advertised only when the server can serve the negotiated extra transport.
Extra connections accept every TSP request allowed for the negotiated TSP version and reject LSP traffic, state-changing notifications, typeServer/connection, and TSP requests not allowed for that version.
Last content update aligned with Pylance 2026.4.1.

title: Cross-request KV cache exposure in the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model, and our remediation with SGLang | Cloudflare Blog
content:
Blog
Security
Workers AI
OCTOBER 26, 2026
Cross-request KV cache exposure in the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model, and our remediation with SGLang
Kevin Flansburg
 and 
Michelle Chen
16 MINUTE READ
COPY URL
On September 8, 2026, we were alerted by a security researcher, Gadi Evron from Knostic, to a tenant isolation issue affecting the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model (@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3) starting on August 27, 2026. We have remediated the issue, and we restored the model on September 9. We have confirmed that no other model hosted on Workers AI was affected.
Between August 27 and September 9, a small number of customers using the GLM 5.3 Workers AI model received responses that contained data from other customers' requests made to the same model shortly before theirs. In total, 155 responses were affected, all to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens.
After excluding our own testing and the researcher's, the requests we identified are consistent in timing and volume with ordinary long-context use, not with someone repeatedly exploiting the bug. We found no evidence of deliberate exploitation.
Today we are publishing this report alongside a post from SGLang, the open-source inference engine that we use, as a coordinated disclosure. This post describes the bug that caused this issue, our response timeline, and the subsequent hardening we have conducted on our production SGLang deployments. We also detail our continued efforts with the upstream maintainers of SGLang to address this and similar bugs.
What happened
GLM is a text generation model from Z.ai that is built for agentic coding workflows; it is one of the many models available through Workers AI. Gadi Evron submitted a report on September 8 through our HackerOne program stating that very long prompts sent to @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 on Workers AI sometimes returned text that belonged to other users' sessions. Cloudflare reproduced the issue the next morning and took the model offline within 40 minutes of declaring an incident. We then deployed a corrected configuration and a patched inference engine, and restored service the same day.  
This specific report of cross-request KV cache exposure was the result of two overlapping issues. The first was a misconfiguration of the open-source inference engine, SGLang, used by Cloudflare. We deployed GLM 5.3 with a 1,048,576-token context window, but the KV cache pool on our prefill GPUs only had room for 681,280 tokens. We were aware of this mismatch before launch. We expected the engine to return an error for any prompt it could not process, and our long-context tests returned successful responses, so we did not believe this to be an issue.
The second was a bug in how SGLang handled the resulting over-length requests in disaggregated prefill/decode mode. A prompt that did not fit the pool was internally marked as rejected and replaced with a one-token placeholder, but instead of aborting the request and returning a client error, prefill generated the KV cache for the placeholder prompt and transferred it to the decode node. The decode node received a "transfer complete" message and assumed that prefill overwrote the KV cache from previous requests with the full prompt for this request, when in fact it left the majority of the previous state intact. The decode node subsequently generated a response while attending over stale cache pages that still held data from earlier requests. As a result, responses to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens could contain data from other users' GLM 5.3 sessions.
Immediate remediation
After disabling the model, we took the following actions to correct this vulnerability before restoring public access to it:
To fix our configuration, we made the pool hold the full context. We adjusted our GLM 5.3 configuration to match our GLM 5.2 configuration, which freed enough GPU memory that the prefill KV pool now holds about 2.04 million tokens, roughly twice the 1,048,576-token context length. A prompt that fits the context window now always fits the pool, so the rejection path is never reached for a valid request. This alone prevents the bug from being exercised.
To fix the engine, we also made the rejection path safe. Relying on pool size alone is fragile: any change to quantization, tensor parallelism, CUDA graph sizes, or a future model version changes the pool size in a way that's easy to miss. Furthermore, there may be other situations in which the prefill scheduler can reject a request and trigger the same bug. To prevent this, we also patched the engine so that a request carrying a pending rejection is retired at the disaggregation admission queue, with its original error, before any bootstrap, allocation, or KV transfer happens. We proposed this upstream as #38704, which also had the decode node verify that the number of tokens transferred matches the number it reserved. The fix was already on SGLang main in #36988, merged September 6 for a related failure path but not yet released. The maintainers also merged #38935, which rejects these requests earlier, following our approach.
We validated both changes against the researcher's reproduction script and our own canary-marker tests before restoring the model.
Background: how we serve GLM 5.3
Workers AI runs GLM 5.3 with SGLang in a disaggregated configuration: a pool of prefill GPUs processes the prompt and produces the model's KV cache for it, then hands that cache over remote direct memory access (RDMA), via Mooncake, to a pool of decode GPUs that generate the response. We have written about this architecture before in our posts on high-performance LLMs and smaller, faster, safer models.
The KV cache in GPU memory is a shared pool of fixed-size pages. Each request is assigned pages when it is admitted and releases them when it finishes. Pages are not currently zeroed between requests; the next request that gets a page simply overwrites it. This approach is common among inference engines and is necessary to achieve the best performance, but it means that the inference engine is responsible for tracking ownership of these memory pages. KV cache page ownership and lifetime tracking has to deal with not just shared ownership within a node (KV cache offload and token generation both access the memory with different lifetimes), but also ownership that is technically shared with the remote prefill node (which holds a simultaneous mutable reference to the page).
Furthermore, the size of this pool is not a configuration value. SGLang sizes it at startup from whatever GPU memory remains after loading the model weights. The model's advertised context length is a separate configuration value. Nothing forces the two to agree, and it is our job to check that they do.
Issue one: misconfiguration
On our GLM 5.3 prefill nodes with our configuration, the pool came to 681,280 tokens while the model's context length is 1,048,576 tokens. The selected KV pool size is printed by SGLang in logs during startup and exposed as a metric. We were aware of this size mismatch; however, during pre-launch testing we observed successful HTTP status codes and a streaming body with no error frames during benchmarking. We assumed that the engine was capable of gracefully handling the difference between the KV cache pool and requested context window via streaming or some other mechanism.
This was one critical gap in our testing: we only validated HTTP response codes and engine performance at long contexts, without validating model output and coherence. We now check KV pool size against context length directly, from the running engine, before any disaggregated deployment change ships, rather than inferring it from response codes.
Issue two: SGLang bug
In v0.5.21, the SGLang team has now addressed this bug in how it was handling prompts longer than the KV pool size. Here’s what was happening before.
When a prompt arrived that was longer than the KV pool could hold, SGLang's scheduler rejected it. The rejection path (Req.set_finish_with_abort) recorded the error to be returned to the client and swapped the prompt for a one-token placeholder so that the request could drain through the normal batch machinery without allocating real memory. On a single-node deployment this worked: the placeholder ran, the batch finished, and the client received an error.
In disaggregated mode such as we operate, the admission queues on both prefill and decode checked whether a request was finished, not whether it was rejected. A rejected request reported itself as live. So:
Bootstrap. The router told the decode node the prompt length (8 pages in the diagram). Decode reserved 8 KV pages for the request.
Prefill admission. The prefill admission queue admitted any request where req.finished() was False. A rejected request stored its rejection in to_finish, not finished_reason, so finished() still returned False. The rejected request was admitted.
Prefill forward pass. Rejection had already replaced the prompt with a one-token placeholder. Prefill ran a trivial forward pass on that one token.
KV transfer. Prefill sent one page of KV to decode and signaled that the transfer was complete.
Decode admission. Decode's admission queue had the same finished() check, so it accepted the handoff.
Decode attention. Decode started generating and attention read all 8 reserved pages. Only page P0 had been written by this request. Pages P1 to P7 still held what earlier requests left in them: other users' prompts and partial generations.
Response. The client got HTTP 200 instead of HTTP 400. prompt_tokens matched the long prompt and the reply was coherent. It arrived faster than an 8-page prefill should take, and it contained content from other users' KV pages.
Every request over the threshold behaved this way. This bug had been reported to SGLang by another user as issue #30233 on July 6, 2026, which Cloudflare noticed while investigating this incident. We had been flagging these types of issues with SGLang since v0.5.10 and this security incident sped up work that Cloudflare had already started in collaboration with the SGLang team. The patch for this issue was released in SGLang v0.5.20, with follow-ups in v0.5.21 and v0.5.22, and is available for all other operators dependent on SGLang to use. We highly recommend all operators update SGLang dependencies to v0.5.22 or later. For more details on specific PRs, read on below.
GLM 5.3 was the only model affected by this bug. Every other disaggregated deployment on Workers AI has KV pools larger than its context length on both prefill and decode, so no request could reach the rejection path. We have applied the engine fix and the hardening described below to every model we serve with SGLang, and our deployment checks require them for every new deployment.
Timeline
All times UTC.
When
What
Aug 27, 2026
GLM 5.3 launched on Workers AI with a prefill KV pool smaller than its context window. The exposure was present from launch.
Sep 8, 2026 - 23:11
Report received via HackerOne.
Sep 9, 2026 - 08:00
Cloudflare begins verifying the HackerOne report.
Sep 9, 2026 - 13:22
Security incident declared. Product Security reproduced the leak using two independent accounts within 25 minutes.
Sep 9, 2026 - 14:00
After confirming the scope of the issue, GLM 5.3 was set to private. Requests return HTTP 400. Status page updated.
Sep 9, 2026 - 14:35
Root cause identified as the prefill pool being smaller than the context length. Canary prefill node with a larger pool confirmed not susceptible.
Sep 9, 2026 - 14:52
All prefill nodes rolled to the corrected configuration.
Sep 9, 2026 - 19:04
Full deployment rebuilt with the corrected configuration plus a Cloudflare-authored engine patch that correctly returns errors for requests rejected by the prefill scheduler. Validated against the researcher's reproduction script.
Sep 9, 2026 - 19:40
Model restored to public.
Sep 10, 2026 - 23:30
Meeting with the SGLang maintainers (RadixArk CTO and core engineers) to agree on upstream fixes.
Sep 11-19, 2026
Additional hardening rolled to all production SGLang deployments (details below).
Sep 16-Oct 12, 2026
Upstream SGLang merges the admission fix, per-transfer checksums, abort-ACK preservation, and turns deferred KV release on by default.
Oct 2, 2026
SGLang v0.5.21 released.
Oct 19, 2026
SGLang v0.5.22 released.
Oct 26, 2026
Coordinated publication with the researcher and RadixArk.
Ongoing hardening effort
This bug belongs to a class of KV cache memory-safety bugs that Cloudflare has been working to address for several months. In each case, a page is freed, reused, or read while something else still has a claim on it. We see two common causes.
The first is page lifetime within a single node. Several tasks on a decode node can hold the same page at once: token generation, offload to host memory, the KV transfer receiver, and the abort and error paths. If one of them frees the page while another is still using it, a new request can be given that page while it is still being read or written. Our earlier fixes for decode offload (#24226, #30899) and double release on grammar errors (#30937) were of this kind.
The second is a race across nodes. When a request is aborted while prefill is still writing its KV cache to decode over RDMA, the writes already sent cannot be recalled. If decode frees those pages right away, those pages can be given to another request, and the late writes land in that request's KV cache. Cloudflare has contributed to the effort to fix this race through proposed fixes (#31357, #38961) and a reproduction script (#32564). In both cases the result is corrupted output, or one user's data in another user's response, with no error raised. The bug in this incident was different: a rejected request went through the handoff every time, rather than by a timing accident. But it had the same result: decode reading pages this request never wrote. None of these covered the failure in this incident in which prefill rejected the request, and decode never learned of it.
Since the incident, we have:
Extended deferred release to hold prefill's source pages as well, and to cover every failure type, not just aborts. We proposed it upstream as #38961, which was superseded by #40645, #41402, and #41404.
Deployed bounded Mooncake transfer batches (#32758, from the SGLang community), so no single transfer call can outlast the release timeout.
Changed our load balancer so a client disconnect no longer aborts a request mid-transfer. It holds the prefill connection until prefill finishes and the decode connection until the first token, then closes both.
Added a check to every disaggregated deployment change: KV pool size measured against context length, deferred release on both roles, transfer batch bounds inside the release timeout, and all required patches applied.
All of these changes were released to our disaggregated production deployments.
Working with the SGLang team
We met with the SGLang maintainers at RadixArk on September

title: APC says let there be light, with raft of standards to speed up photonics manufacturing
content:
CONNECT
APC Says Let There Be Light, With Raft Of Standards To Speed Up Photonics Manufacturing
Joe Fay
Published fri 23 Oct 2026 // 12:46 UTC
The Advanced Photonics Coalition has given the green light for a slew of standards it says should allow “high volume manufacturing” of optical networking kit.
The announcement, at the PECC Summit earlier this week, comes amidst concerns about shortages of key components and materials needed for manufacturing optical networking gear, even as the surging AI industry starts hitting the “copper wall.” As Gbps demands rise, copper’s reach gets ever shorter, while heat emissions and energy consumption increases.
But the photonics industry is struggling to scale. Earlier this month, Lumentum Holdings told Bloomberg that its optical components are “completely sold out” through to 2029, and it won’t be able to meet demand for some products between now and 2028. The company produces indium phosphide components which are critical for photonics. China is a major producer of indium phosphide adding an extra level of geopolitical stress to the supply chain.
Lumentum’s backers include Nvidia, whose founder and CEO Jensen Huang demonstrated its Spectrum X co-packaged optics-based technology at GTC this week.
“So we now have extremely high data rate, extremely high quality data that comes directly onto the chip, and this goes directly into transceivers without going through a PCB and a transceiver goes right into the optics,” enthused Huang.
More broadly, datacenter operators are banking on optical to deliver more data to their pricey GPUs and increase efficiency as the technology requires less power and produces less heat.
Earlier this month, McKinsey flagged networking as one of the areas that “requires improvement” as AI becomes more and more about inference, advising operators “deploy optics-integrated switches (CPO) for higher bandwidth density and lower power per bit.” And it flagged up the need for “open interconnect” saying “a specialized architecture only earns it cost at volume.”
But statements like Lumentum’s raise the fear that optical networking components are heading towards the sort of shortages – and surging prices - already plaguing high end DRAM and flash storage.
The APC said this week that “By establishing common manufacturing, interface, and test practices, APC aims to remove implementation variations that add no market value and overcome supply chain silos that constrain volume.”
Its standards portfolio “supports multiple sourcing and broader supplier participation, helping the industry build an open and scalable photonics ecosystem.”
The portfolio covers:
• System Level Architecture Overview for Co-Packaged Optics
• Co-Packaged Optics Informative Outlook and Recommended Practices
• Silicon Photonics for Co-Packaged Optics Recommended Test Practices
• 4-Core Multicore Fiber Cable, Connector and Fiber Array Unit Specification
• Silicon Photonics Manufacturing Specification
Photonics developer Resolight is one of the companies on the APC working group.
“There are two technologies that today are independent and actually co-deployed in scale up,” said Ofer Shapiro, Resolight CEO. “One is traditional slow switching OCS that they're using to reconfigure the network. And the other one is data switches that are working 1,000 times faster.”
Resolight sees the APC standards as an endorsement of its Nanosecond optical circuit switching approach, addressing the protocol integration needed to enable native photon routing through nanosecond optical circuit switching (OCS).
“Native photon routing extends optical switching into the data plane itself, directing coordinated data transfers through the network while keeping their payloads in the light domain,” it said in a statement.
By reducing repeated optical to electrical to optical conversions, its architecture could deliver a massive boost in network energy efficiency and dramatically reduce the number of optical transceivers needed in multi-rack AI scaleup networks.
“The APC CPO specifications address the data-plane integration needed to make native photon routing a practical alternative to electronic data switching,” Shapiro added in Resolight’s statement.
“The easiest to source and the greenest transceiver is the one that you don't need,” Shapiro told us.
He added that if Indium Phosphide supplies were a concern, the sensible response was to “need less of it rather than figure out where do we get more.”
In its "Co-Packaged Optics Informative Outlook and Recommended Practices" document released this week, the APC said, “Without open ecosystem driven standards, the natural gravitational pull is toward vertically integrated proprietary solutions, an outcome that would fragment the market, increase customer lock-in risk, slow adoption, and ultimately diminish the opportunities of innovation for CPO’s technical benefits.”
When it comes to Nanosecond-Level OCS, it said: “The objective is not to standardize a particular fast OCS implementation, but to define the control-plane, optical-interface and behavioral framework that allows fast, transparent OCS to operate as a first-class component of an open AI scale-up fabric.
Earlier this year, Chris Sharp, the chief technology officer at data centre operator Digital Realty, told the BBC, "I think we're at the end of copper" with networking increasingly becoming the key factor slowing down compute.
CONNECT

title: CSS-Tricks has a new owner! | CSS-Tricks
content:
CSS-TRICKS NEWS
CSS-TRICKS HAS A NEW OWNER!
By Geoff Graham on Oct 26, 2026
This is pretty wild, but let’s get right to it because it’s big news:
CSS-Tricks is an independent site once again!
Just to recap: DigitalOcean purchased CSS-Tricks in 2022 from Chris Coyier, who founded the site in 2007. Chris ran it all the way up to that purchase.
Here we are in 2026, and I’m taking independent ownership of the site.
So, wait, who owns the site? That’d be me. (Wow, never imagined I would get to say that!) Of course, I have a small, awesome team to help with the day-to-day management of the site.
That all said, I do envision that some things will change. In fact, I’m planning that they will change in what I hope are very good ways. Maybe a question-answer thing makes sense here since this is very much an evolving discussion.
Do you, like, own the site now?
Yes, I’ve got the keys to the castle, so to speak. And, even after 12 years of working on the site, I’ll admit I’m a little overwhelmed and nervous about that. I mean, it’s an investment for sure, as you can imagine, and I’m making this my full-time job. At least for a while.
I want to make CSS-Tricks both a real community and a place that’s inclusive of everyone, no matter where they are in their front-end learning journey. That’s going to take some work and time.
How can you afford this?
My latest IPO launched, and I’m now worth one trillion dollars. Wait, wait. That’s not right.
It’s going to be hard. Advertising will certainly be needed now. But, in order to keep the lights on, I’ll have to approach them differently.
In the pre-DigitalOcean days we sold real ad packages with things like display ads, sponsored posts, newsletter sponsors, and the like. As an independent website, we will need to return to our advertising roots. 
So, if you’re in a place looking to advertise, please do reach out! 
LOL, advertising.
Right?! Ad revenue can’t be the only thing paying the bills. I have lots of ideas and several plates already spinning. Like, I’ve been neck deep in developing an HTML/CSS course for beginners. 
(And you can now support the site by becoming a member — thanks in advance!)
LOL, courses.
Educational content has been in the dumps lately, right? Again, I’m hoping that CSS-Tricks will be more inclusive, no matter where you or anyone else is at in the learning journey. This place has traditionally been for folks who know what they’re doing. But I’m truly committed to creating more entry points for those getting started, particularly as our field is in the early throes of a growing skills gap.
And yes, I do believe that learning the basics is more important now than ever. But what learning actually looks like is what’s key. Front-end courses are down across the board. It has to be done differently.
There are other things in the works, but I think a course is one of the first things you’ll see. 
Oh, and the newsletter. That’s coming back after a way-too-long hiatus.
What about publishing new articles?
That’s still very much a thing! We’ll keep our regularly scheduled broadcast going.
But maybe a little less than you’re used to. Those articles are part of the investment I’m making. Expect maybe one or two articles most weeks, at least as the ball starts rolling.
That also means the guest writing form is back in business! We have a nice backlog of articles through the rest of the year, which is great, but also means new submissions will have to wait a bit.
I won’t be able to accept everything that comes in, but I will absolutely read them and follow-up as best I can. Unless it’s a slop submission, of course.
Will you be writing most of the articles to save cost?
Nah! My goal is to make CSS-Tricks a platform that gives folks a voice to share great ideas. I think we all prefer that over me just using it as my own soapbox. I’ve written plenty for this site the past 12 years. I’m happier (and more comfortable) being behind the curtain and giving others the full spotlight.
I may be writing a bit, developing the site here and there, editing a small stack of article drafts, or helping with sponsorships. I gag at the thought of titles, but publisher hits best for me. My fingers are in all the bowls, but my most important responsibilities are:
Helping writers develop a voice, and
giving them a platform to use that voice, so that
they help others get a little better at their jobs.
The best thing I can possibly do is help folks develop a voice and give them a stage to use it. It’s about community and culture building. Publisher. That’s more my jam.
Can I support you in some way?
You totally can. I put a little membership deal together where you can join a members-only community on Discord along with some perks. Or check out the new shop. Or purchase advertising for your company. In the near-future you will be able to purchase the aforementioned course as well. Any little bit helps, of course. I squirm at the thought of asking for money, so there’s no pressure.
Support doesn’t even have to be financial! We all know that content publishers need all the eyeballs we can get in these prompt-filled days. Things like subscribing to the newsletter, sharing articles you like with others, clicking through from your RSS app, and checking out our sponsors are all very, very great ways to support us.
I have so many thoughts about this.
Yeah, me too. This post could go on and on. I’m an open book, though, and I’m happy to answer anything you might have in the comments. I know, so 2015, right?
Here we go!

title: 'It's offensively cheap': How solar power is quietly becoming bigger than nuclear
content:
'It's offensively cheap': How solar power is quietly becoming bigger than nuclear
20 hours ago
Share
Save
Add as preferred on Google
Jocelyn Timperley
Getty Images
(Credit: Getty Images)
After defying projections, solar's dramatic growth means it is now overtaking nuclear as a global power source. Here are seven reasons for solar's success, and where it might go from here.
The world's solar power is crossing a threshold. A decade ago, it barely registered on a global scale, providing just 1% of the world's power. In 2026, it will almost certainly increase to 10% of power, and overtake nuclear, a mainstay of electricity since the late 1970s.
Globally, solar electricity generation quietly overtook nuclear power (just) in 2025, according to statistics from UK-based energy think tank Ember. And BBC analysis of Ember data over the past 12 months up to September 2026 shows it clearly outstripping nuclear, producing 13% more power.
"[Solar] generating more electricity than all the world's nuclear power plants is a pretty insane stat, for sure," says Dave Jones, co-founder of Ember. 
From China's vast arrays to a recent solar upsurge driven by escalating oil prices, the incredible rise of solar power has defied all projections. Here are seven ways it has become an apparently "unstoppable force" – and what the future looks like from here.
ADVERTISEMENT
1. An underestimated force 
"Solar is now the engine of the power transition," says Jan Rosenow, a professor of energy and climate policy at the University of Oxford in the UK.
Solar has become the fastest-growing source of new electricity in history, and by far the largest source of new electricity globally. In 2025, it met three-quarters of the growth in the world's demand for electricity, overtaking wind power generation (wind power is also growing, just a little more slowly).
That's where solar's going, to not just be king of electricity, but king of energy – Dave Jones
"It wasn't expected," says Rosenow. Mainstream projections, he says, have underestimated solar year after year. Outlooks such as those from the International Energy Agency (IEA), an influential intergovernmental organisation based in Paris, "assumed linear growth and slowly falling costs, and got both wrong".
Over 2026, multiple sources indicate solar electricity generation will almost certainly far exceed nuclear globally. Nuclear's electricity generation has remained more or less constant since 2000, while solar's has increased some 2,700-fold.
Ember/ BBC
Ember data shows solar electricity generation narrowly surpassing nuclear in 2025. In 2026, it will almost certainly well exceed it (Credit: Ember/BBC)
2. 'Offensively cheap'
Solar, a mature technology for some 15 years now, became the cheapest electricity in history in 2020. Since then, solar has scaled, efficiency has risen, and the amount of silicon and silver used in panels has gone down, leading prices to fall yet further, says Jones. 
"Massive Chinese manufacturing scale and current overcapacity have pushed module prices to record lows," says Rosenow. 
In particular, a large fall in the price of panels in 2023-24 pushed us into the current era of what Jones calls "offensively cheap" solar. "A panel in itself is just so unbelievably cheap," he says. "It's well under $100 (£75)… and that's going to keep you generating electricity for 30, 40 years without any input at all."
Of course, it's not just in purely economic terms that solar is bringing down costs. Researchers have calculated the US's rising wind and solar generation brought it $249bn (£186bn) in climate and health benefits between 2019 and 2022.
3. Global uptake
China is still the world's biggest solar power by far but is by no means the only player.
Despite the US imposing a variety of tariffs on solar, it remains the second country when it comes to installations, which are still skyrocketing – especially in states won by President Trump in 2024. In fact, the US now has enough solar to power more than one-third of its households.
"Tariffs and other federal policies that constrain renewable energy growth are certainly expected to raise costs and slow expansion relative to what we otherwise would have seen," says Alicia Zhao, an expert in US mitigation pathways at the University of Maryland. 
"However, economics are a key part of why solar has been able to grow so quickly. Even with rising costs, solar is still one of the cheapest sources of new power in the US. And it is getting built regardless of political lines."
Getty Images
China's internal solar boom is now slowing down, but its cheap solar exports to other countries are still increasing (Credit: Getty Images)
India, meanwhile, is moving away from fossil fuels far faster than China did, and new solar has met 60% of its rise in power demand in the past two years.
In Australia, over four million homes now have rooftop solar: well over a third of all households.
4. Unreliable fossil fuels
Countries like Pakistan and Lebanon have also begun installing solar at breakneck speeds, while across Africa countries are installing some 100,000 solar panels per day.
In many places, escalating diesel prices, driven by the Russia-Ukraine conflict and US-Israel war with Iran, has swung the cost needle yet further in solar's favour. This is especially the case in many African countries where home diesel generators are a mainstay due to unreliable grids. Rooftop solar panels, nearly all of them imported from China, have now taken off as an alternative.
Ethiopia has even banned the import of petrol and diesel cars in a bid to tackle oil dependency and pollution, says Jones.
Solar is also rapidly providing new electricity where fossil-based grids can't keep up with demand. Pakistan, for example, has become a surprising poster child for the solar revolution due to its extraordinarily rapid rise in installations. In 2019, solar provided less than 2% of its electricity; now it's 24%, driven by costly, unreliable grid electricity combined and cheap solar imports from China.
"What's really incredible in Pakistan is… generally most of the solar boom has been out of people's pockets," says Jones. "People can afford it, without needing to take out loans."
A similar story has been seen in several other "sun belt" countries, from Lebanon to Nigeria. "[Solar] lets households act without waiting for governments or utilities," says Rosenow. "In uncertain times, that speed and independence is extremely valuable."
5. Battery revolution
Solar power, of course, can only be produced during the day when the sun is shining. To turn it into electricity that can be dispatched at any time, it needs to be paired with batteries.
Fortunately, batteries have been having their own cost revolution, transforming their ability to support the solar rollout. "Solar plus storage is now routinely cheaper than new fossil plants in sunny regions," says Rosenow. "Batteries have largely solved the daily problem of shifting midday sun into the evening."
Alamy
Solar has gone from Pakistan's fifth-largest electricity source in 2023 to its largest in 2025, says Rosenow (Credit: Alamy)
In California, for example, solar and batteries met on average over a quarter of electricity demand from 19:00-21:00 (the evening peak) over the first half of 2026. US states such as Vermont are now rolling out grid-integrated systems of home batteries, often paired with solar.
Barriers still remain for longer-term storage of solar across seasons, cloudy periods and monsoon seasons, though, both Rosenow and Jones say. It means the integration of solar into the wider electricity system still matters, says Rosenow.
6. Electrify everything
Solar is seen as a key part of the push towards electrification, reducing fossil fuel use in areas that previously didn't use electricity, such as via electric cars. Electrification has been chosen as a major theme at this year's UN climate talks in Turkey.
"That's where solar's going, to not just be king of electricity, but king of energy," says Jones. 
Still, it all requires a plan, Julia Souder, chief executive of the Long Duration Energy Storage Council, a global executive-led non-profit established at COP26, warned recently. "There is an inherent danger in uncontrolled electrification, and adding massive new loads without built-in flexibility creates a fragile system," she wrote in a blog for international policy network Ren21. "Electrification is not automatically resilient." 
The limits on solar are now grids, storage and how fast we electrify demand, says Rosenow – not panels or cost. "The bigger question is no longer whether solar grows but whether our power systems and institutions can keep up."
In the US, data centres and electrification mean power demand is growing for the first time in decades, says Zhao, with energy security a national priority. 
"Renewables already make up over 90% of new capacity in the US," she says. "This need for secure, quickly deployable electricity could create a critical opportunity for [further] renewable energy growth even without support from the current federal government."
7. Expanding tech
In the past few years, plug-in panels (or "balcony solar"), have started spreading rapidly in Germany. These generate less electricity than rooftop panels but feed it directly into homes via a standard socket.
They have now been approved in several other countries and US states including California.
Meanwhile, agrivoltaics, which combines food production and solar panels, is being touted as a solution to concerns in some areas about the land use of solar.
Getty Images
In Kentucky, US, a solar ranch pays a local farmer to graze his sheep among its solar panels, producing pasture-fed meat while keeping grass and weeds down (Credit: Getty Images)
Other technologies from floating and "mirror" solar plants to perovskite panels and solar windows could all see growth in coming years.
What's next for solar
In 2026, the world's solar capacity will go on rising, but the rate of expansion may slow down for the first time ever, says Jones.
This is down to China: last summer, it changed its regime for managing and supporting new solar installations, leading to a burst of installations in 2025 to fall under the old price regime. Elsewhere, it's a different picture. "If you exclude China, there's more panels being installed this year than last year," says Jones.
By 2030, the IEA thinks solar power generation will have reached double that of 2025's levels, with solar overtaking hydro to become the world's third-largest electricity source.
"Wherever grid power is costly and unreliable, the economics keep pulling people towards solar," says Rosenow. "There is one caveat: if Chinese solar panels are difficult to import this will not happen at speed." 
More like this:
• The US state replacing power plants with home batteries
• The dream of beaming solar energy from orbit
• Perovskite: The 'wonder material' that could transform solar 
There has been a lot of bad news about the climate recently. It's now incredibly likely the 1.5C global limit set in Paris in 2015 will be breached, the world is seeing rising climate impacts and is edging towards several climate tipping points this century.
But the solar success story shows we are also making progress in ways that were never anticipated. A decade ago, "no one was getting close to expecting that to happen", says Jones, noting that the growth in clean electricity has directly translated to fewer coal plants being built. 
"Now, worst cases [of climate change] are somewhere between 2-3C of warming, rather than 4C of warming."
