LISPy things you can do in 64K bytes of core
where "in 64K bytes" shall mean 64K bytes for the LISP system, the runtime stack, and the cons pool! This is the amount of space your LISP system would get on a basic DEC PDP-11 or in a tiny-model PCDOS program. It is probably a little less space than the first implementations of LISP could use.
The IBM 704 electronic data processing machine at M.I.T., on which LISP was first implemented in 1960, had 32K words of 36-bit core memory, [1] which in this case really means one tiny ferrite ring per bit. So there was a total of 36×32768=1,183,608 tiny little toroids housed in a not so tiny steel frame. The 704 required a rather spacious room with reinforced floors and industrial air conditioning. The total weight of a typical installation was around 10 metric tons.
The LISP system itself occupied 12K words of core and one word would hold a complete cons cell, [1] so the machine offered a little less than 20K cells of space to LISP. But then, the IBM 704 at the M.I.T. was quite a well-equipped machine. Many 704 installations included as little as 8K words or even 4K words of memory [2] — too little to run a LISP system. Here is a LISP 1.0 sample program from [1]:
DEFINE
(( (SUBST (LAMBDA (X Y Z) (COND ((ATOM Z) (COND ((EQ Y Z) X)
(T Z))) (T (CONS (SUBST X Y (CAR Z)) (SUBST X Y (CDR Z))))))) ))
()
Note that programs were usually typed on as few lines as possible, because they had to be punched to punched cards or typed in at a teletype which echoed its input on paper. The operator (DEFINE), the arguments (in double parentheses in the case of DEFINE), and an environment had to be supplied to the LISP system in three separate expressions.
There were smaller computers running LISP, though. In 1964 there was PDP-1 LISP, which was an implementation for DEC's PDP-1 computer and it ran on systems with as little as 4096 words of 18-bit storage, where the system itself used around 2000 words. [3] Even on the PDP-1 a cons cell would fit in a single word, so some 2000 cells were available to the system. Here is a PDP-1 LISP sample program from [3] — yes, PDP-1 LISP used lower case:
(rplacd (quote r1) (quote (expr (lambda (m l) (cond ((null l) m)
     (t (r1 (cons (car l) m) (cdr l))))))))
(rplacd (quote reverse) (quote (expr (lambda (l) (r1 nil l)))))
The LISP system that will be used in the following is Kilo LISP, which is a portable implementation written in ANSI C (C89) that can compile to a tiny model PCDOS executable that runs in 64K bytes of memory. The LISP system itself occupies about 13K bytes, leaving enough space for 8192 cons cells, where each cell allocates 5 bytes (16 bits car, 16 bits cdr, and 3 bits tag, the latter rounded up to 8 bits). Here is a sample program:
(setq assoc
  (lambda (x a)
    (cond ((null a) nil)
          ((eq x (caar a)) (car a))
          (else (assoc x (cdr a))))))
The Kilo LISP system offers less than half as many cons cells as a big IBM 704 installation and about four times the space of a minimal PDP-1. Of course, ancient computers were slow: the IBM 704 had a clock speed of 40kHz (0.04 MIPS) and the PDP-1 operated at 150kHz (0.15 MIPS), but then the LISP systems on those machines were carefully hand-crafted assembly language programs and their hardware would typically execute one instruction per clock cycle.
Today you can probably emulate an IBM 704 and a PDP-1 on a cheap smartphone, both running at a multiple of the speed of the original hardware, while playing your favorite jump-and-run game. So while a 704 or a PDP-1 could probably run all of the following example programs, they would certainly take their time. The rest of this essay will concentrate on the memory aspect and ignore run times.
Here is a first impression of what ancient LISP feels like.

content:

Pharo 14 Released!
Dear Pharo users and dynamic language lovers:
We have released Pharo version 14!
What is Pharo?
Pharo is a pure object-oriented programming language and a powerful environment focused on simplicity and immediate feedback.
Screenshot of Pharo 14
Simple & powerful language: No constructors, no types declaration, no interfaces, no primitive types. Yet a powerful and elegant language with a full syntax fitting in one postcard! Pharo is objects and messages all the way down.
Live, immersive environment: Immediate feedback at any moment of your development: Developing, testing, debugging. Even in production environments, you will never be stuck in compiling and deploying steps again!
Amazing debugging experience: Pharo environment includes a debugger unlike anything you've seen before. It allows you to step through code, restart the execution of methods, create methods on the fly, and much more!
Pharo is yours: Pharo is made by an incredible community, with more than [X] contributors for the last revision of the platform and hundreds of people constantly contributing with frameworks and libraries.
Fully open-source: Pharo full stack is released under MIT License and available on GitHub
... more on the Pharo Features page.
In this iteration of Pharo, our efforts have concentrated on three main areas:
Modernizing the development tools. We introduced Mission Control and Pulse (the replacement for Spotter), reworked the Method Browser and rewrote the Settings Browser, and consolidated Epicea and ProfStef into NewTools. This continues our ongoing migration of the development tools to the Spec-based tooling stack.
Rebuilding the refactoring and command infrastructure. Refactoring commands were migrated to a driver-based architecture behind a unified command registry, and we kept expanding Pharo's command-line capabilities (command-line testing, a command-line debugger, and Sindarin script tooling).
Modernizing the virtual machine. We unified frames and stack management, added RISC-V JIT support, extended memory management (direct old-space allocation and GC improvements), advanced Slang/C compilation, and modernized the cross-platform build infrastructure.
Worth noting: starting with this release, we have moved our release schedule from spring (March–May) to fall (September–November). Pharo 14 is the first version released under the new schedule.

title: Is PHP Quietly Running on Your ColdFusion Server? How to Check, and Remove It
content:
Is PHP Quietly Running on Your ColdFusion Server? How to Check, and Remove It
OCT
23
Blog
Tech
ColdFusion
Server Administration
by Gregory Alexander

If you run ColdFusion or Lucee on a Windows server with IIS, and you've never installed PHP on purpose, this one's for you. There's a good chance PHP is on your server. It may be left behind by a control panel, a phpMyAdmin install from years ago, or your host's setup image. Here's how to find out in a few minutes with PowerShell, and how to remove it safely if nothing uses it.
I remember when I could go years without applying a security fix. Now it feels like I'm chasing something down every few weeks: a patch here, a mitigation there, a bot hammering a page that shouldn't exist. Such is life in the AI era, sigh. 
While I was signing in to my test blog the other day, the admin page refused me with a plain IIS error: 403 Forbidden, and a message saying multipart form-data requests were blocked by a PHP mitigation. My blogs are ColdFusion. They don't run a single line of PHP. So why was a PHP security rule stopping me from signing in?
Table of Contents
What happened
Check 1: is IIS sending .php files to PHP?
Check 2: are there any PHP files in your sites?
Check 3: is PHP installed or running?
Check 4: what can the internet see?
Removing it safely
If you need to keep a rule like this
Lucee on Linux and Apache
Gotchas
Further Reading
What happened
The timing wasn't a coincidence. On October 21, 2026, PHP shipped emergency patches for two critical flaws that let an unauthenticated request run code on the server, nicknamed PHP2Shell. Every PHP setup that serves web requests was affected: PHP-FPM, Apache's mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. The fix is to install a new version of PHP (8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35).
My hosting company responded the same week with a web server security rule. The rule lived in IIS's server-wide URL Rewrite rules, so it applied to every site on the server and blocked every request whose content type was multipart/form-data, regardless of the address. That's the encoding a browser uses for any form that can upload a file, and plenty of forms use it even when they don't.
PHP's own advice doesn't include blocking those requests. It's to patch, and until then to turn off session.upload_progress.enabled and lower post_max_size. Several of the official mitigations concern how PHP handles uploads, so I can see why a host would reach for the biggest hammer. For a PHP site that's a blunt but understandable shield. For my ColdFusion sites it meant the admin sign-in form, every image upload and every file upload failed on all four sites at once. The rule matched every address, not just .php ones.
Once I'd scoped the rule to .php addresses (more on that below), everything worked again. Then I asked the obvious question: why is PHP on this server at all? The answer was a phpMyAdmin install I had asked for years ago to manage one MySQL database. It was still there, still in a site folder, and its login page was open to the whole internet. The host turned the blanket rule off once I told them PHP was no longer in use, and I went looking for anything else PHP had left behind.
Check 1: is IIS sending .php files to PHP?
IIS only runs PHP if a handler mapping tells it to. Open PowerShell as Administrator on the server:
Import-Module WebAdministration
Get-WebHandler -PSPath 'IIS:\Sites' | Where-Object { $_.path -like '*.php' } | Select-Object name, path, scriptProcessor
PowerShell (Windows)Copy
If it prints nothing, IIS doesn't run PHP. If it prints something like this, it does, for every site that inherits the server's settings:
name    path  scriptProcessor
----    ----  ---------------
FastCGI *.php C:\php\php-cgi.exe
Plain textCopy
Note the handler's name and the scriptProcessor path. You'll need both if you remove it.
Check 2: are there any PHP files in your sites?
PowerShell's Get-ChildItem -Recurse works, but on a server with years of uploaded images it can crawl for minutes. Windows' own dir is much faster. This counts the PHP files under your web root:
cmd /c "dir C:\inetpub\wwwroot\*.php /s /b" 2>$null | Measure-Object | Select-Object Count
PowerShell (Windows)Copy
If the count isn't zero, this shows which folders they're in, busiest first:
cmd /c "dir C:\inetpub\wwwroot\*.php /s /b" 2>$null | ForEach-Object { Split-Path $_ -Parent } | Group-Object | Sort-Object Count -Descending | Select-Object -First 25 Count, Name | Format-Table -AutoSize
PowerShell (Windows)Copy
Mine found about 4,500 files in two folders, both phpMyAdmin: one inside a site, and a second copy at the web root, which IIS's Default Web Site served to anyone who visited the server's bare IP address.
If you find PHP files you don't recognize, especially scattered through image or upload folders, or changed recently, stop and treat it as a possible break-in. Attackers love dropping small PHP "web shells" into upload folders. This lists the most recently changed ones:
cmd /c "dir C:\inetpub\wwwroot\*.php /s /b" 2>$null | Get-Item | Sort-Object LastWriteTime -Descending | Select-Object -First 15 LastWriteTime, Length, FullName | Format-Table -AutoSize
PowerShell (Windows)Copy
Check 3: is PHP installed or running?
Get-Process php* -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object Name, Id, StartTime
Test-Path C:\php
PowerShell (Windows)Copy
No php-cgi.exe process just means nothing has asked for a PHP page recently. IIS starts it on demand. The handler from Check 1 is what matters.
Check 4: what can the internet see?
From any computer, try the usual addresses on your own sites:
foreach ($path in "phpmyadmin/", "phpMyAdmin/", "pma/", "info.php") {
    $url = "https://www.mysite.com/$path"
    try { $r = Invoke-WebRequest $url -UseBasicParsing -TimeoutSec 15; "$($r.StatusCode) $url" }
    catch { "$($_.Exception.Response.StatusCode.value__) $url" }
}
PowerShell (Windows)Copy
Anything that answers 200 deserves a look. A phpMyAdmin login page facing the internet is a standing invitation: bots try passwords on it all day, and every attempt starts PHP and talks to your database.
Removing it safely
Do these in order, and back up first. Every step is reversible.
1. Back up IIS's configuration
IIS can snapshot its own configuration and restore it in one command:
& "$env:windir\System32\inetsrv\appcmd.exe" add backup "before-php-removal"
PowerShell (Windows)Copy
To undo everything below: appcmd.exe restore backup "before-php-removal".
2. Move phpMyAdmin (and any other PHP app) out of the web folders
Move, don't delete. Its configuration file may hold a database password, so keep it somewhere private for a few weeks in case something turns out to need it:
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force C:\Temp\removed-php | Out-Null
Move-Item C:\inetpub\wwwroot\mysite\phpmyadmin C:\Temp\removed-php\phpmyadmin-mysite
PowerShell (Windows)Copy
If Move-Item complains that a file is in use, PHP has it open. iisreset /stop, move it, then iisreset /start. (Your sites are down for a few seconds.) And if it says "Could not find a part of the path", it's the destination folder that's missing, not the source. That one fooled me.
For managing MySQL afterwards, a desktop tool on the server over Remote Desktop, like HeidiSQL or MySQL Workbench, does everything phpMyAdmin did without a public login page.
3. Block .php at the door
IIS's request filtering can turn away a file extension before any handler sees it. Added at the server level, it covers every site:
Add-WebConfigurationProperty -PSPath 'MACHINE/WEBROOT/APPHOST' -Filter 'system.webServer/security/requestFiltering/fileExtensions' -Name '.' -Value @{ fileExtension = '.php'; allowed = 'false' }
PowerShell (Windows)Copy
Now any .php address gets "404 - the request filtering module is configured to deny the file extension", whether the file exists or not.
4. Remove the handler and the FastCGI entry
Use the handler name from Check 1 (mine was FastCGI) and the php-cgi.exe path:
Remove-WebConfigurationProperty -PSPath 'MACHINE/WEBROOT/APPHOST' -Filter 'system.webServer/handlers' -Name '.' -AtElement @{ name = 'FastCGI' }
Remove-WebConfigurationProperty -PSPath 'MACHINE/WEBROOT/APPHOST' -Filter 'system.webServer/fastCgi' -Name '.' -AtElement @{ fullPath = 'C:\php\php-cgi.exe' }
PowerShell (Windows)Copy
Run Check 1 again. It should print nothing.
5. Uninstall PHP, last
If PHP came from an installer, remove it under Apps > Installed apps. If it's just a folder like C:\php, rename it to C:\php-removed for a few weeks before deleting it. If anything complains, you'll know right away, and it's one rename to put back.
If PHP was installed by your host, ask them before step 5. Their own monitoring scripts are unlikely to need it, but it's their install.
If you need to keep a rule like this
Maybe you do run PHP somewhere, or your host wants their rule. Then scope it to PHP addresses instead of every address. The rule's <match url=".*" /> was the whole problem. This changes it to .php addresses only, leaving ColdFusion's forms alone (use the rule's own name):
Set-WebConfigurationProperty -PSPath 'MACHINE/WEBROOT/APPHOST' -Filter "system.webServer/rewrite/globalRules/rule[@name='PHP Mitigation']/match" -Name url -Value '\.php($|/)'
PowerShell (Windows)Copy
Note the single quotes around the pattern. I first tried the same change with appcmd.exe, and PowerShell quietly mangled the quoting: no error, and no change either. Set-WebConfigurationProperty with single quotes did it on the first try. Check the result with Select-String on C:\Windows\System32\inetsrv\config\applicationHost.config.
Lucee on Linux and Apache
The same questions, different commands:
php -v                          ## is the PHP command-line installed?
apachectl -M | grep -i php      ## is Apache running PHP (php_module, proxy_fcgi to php-fpm)?
find /var/www /home -name "*.php" 2>/dev/null | head -50
Bash (Linux, macOS)Copy
On Debian and Ubuntu, sudo a2dismod php8.3 (your version) and sudo systemctl restart apache2 stop Apache from running PHP. Then remove the packages with your package manager once you're sure nothing needs them. Control panels such as Virtualmin often install PHP for their own tools, so check before uninstalling.
Gotchas
A server-wide rule catches every site. A rule written for PHP blocked my ColdFusion sign-ins and uploads. If a 403 appears out of nowhere, read the full IIS error page; mine named the rule.
Hosts re-run their scripts. Mine recreated its rule on every run, so a local fix could have been undone silently. Tell your host what you changed and why.
A config edit can land in the wrong web.config. My first fix went into a site's web.config, and nothing changed. A quick Select-String on the file IIS actually reads would have saved me ten minutes.
Trusted Cache hides your fixes. If you replace a .cfm by hand while diagnosing, ColdFusion keeps running the old compiled copy until you clear it. A brand-new file name is the quick workaround.
Removing PHP isn't a substitute for patching. If you do run PHP, update it now to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35 (or newer), and set session.upload_progress.enabled = 0 in php.ini until you can. PHP 8.1 and older no longer get updates from the PHP project. Removing PHP is only the right answer when nothing uses it.
Further Reading
PHP's announcements for October 2026, including the October 21 security releases and their mitigations: php.net news archive, 2026
BleepingComputer: PHP ships emergency patches for critical PHP2Shell flaws
PHP on Windows has been here before. DEVCORE's alert for the 2024 PHP-CGI flaw: Security Alert: CVE-2024-4577, PHP CGI Argument Injection Vulnerability
Charlie Arehart: ColdFusion Lockdown/Security guides - there are several, and some you may have missed. Old, but still the best map of the lockdown guides, and it points at IIS request filtering.
Adobe's lockdown guides: ColdFusion 2025 Lockdown Guide and ColdFusion 2023 Lockdown Guide (PDFs)
Microsoft's IIS reference: File Name Extensions (request filtering), Handlers and FastCGI

title: retronetworking | retronetworking.org
content:
retronetworking
Also available in: Deutsch
Historical Telecommunications
We're a loose collective of fairly technical people with an interest in historical telecommunications.
There is [so far] no legal entity behind this effort; it's just the collaboration of various individuals with a common goal. We spend our own money on acquiring historical artifacts and invest our spare time in documenting, repairing and researching them.
Most [large, public] telecommunications museums are rather disappointing from our view, as they are way too superficial and often happy with exhibiting some dead piece of hardware with a one-page description. What we are missing in many museums is equipment that is operational, as well as deeper knowledge about the context in which it was built, its internal operation, the major components it uses, the full user manuals, etc.
Furthermore, many communications museums focus on more early forms of electronic communications in the sense of analog telephony networks, electromechanical switching, telephones, telegraphs, etc. - while our main focus is more on the digital communications technology, roughly from the late 1960s through the late 1990s.
Goals / Activities
Our goals (and activities to reach those goals) are to
assemble, digitize, archive and publish information about historical [digital] telecommunications technologies, including
data sheets, user manuals, service manuals, schematics, firmware updates, etc. for end-user, network-side transmission and switching equipment
historical journals, books, articles, brochures and magazines about the respective technologies
collect, document, maintain, operate and exhibit historical [digital] telecommunications equipment
take high-resolution images of the equipment (both exterior and of all circuit boards) and publish them online
exhibit some of the equipment at certain events like vintage computing fairs/festivals or hacker conferences
develop, build and operate emulators for historical telecommunications networks to enable interested parties to operate their historical equipment against a simulated network over the internet
provide places online (such as chat, forum, mailing lists, video conferences) by which interested people can get in touch and collaborate within the goals of our project.
Areas of Interest
Areas of interest include (but are not limited to):
PCM (Pulse Code Modulation) transmission technology
CSPDNs (Circuit-Switched Public Data Networks) like German Datex-L
PSPDNs (Packet-Switched Public Data Networks) based on X.25 like German Datex-P
ISDN (Integrated Services Digital Network)
Digital Telephone Switching (EWSD, System 12, System X, AXE, ...)
Frame Relay
DQDB
PDH (Plesiochronous Digital Hierarchy)
SDH (Synchronous Digital Hierarchy)
ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode)

title: UK to charge universities $1,200 per international student, including those from Nigeria, Kenya, India and Pakistan, targeting $594 million in first-year revenue | Business Insider Africa
content:
Graduation ceremony of a university in the UK [Getty Images]
From August 2028, universities in England will pay an annual levy of £925 for each international student beyond an exemption threshold of 220 students.
The charge applies to institutions recruiting from countries including China, India, Nigeria, Pakistan, and Bangladesh, and covers both new and existing students.
While students do not pay the fee directly, universities may increase international tuition fees to recover their costs, affecting future pricing strategies.
University leaders have criticized the levy due to concerns over declining international student numbers and potential financial strain, though the government insists the measure supports education funding.

First announced in the government's 2025 Budget, the International Student Levy has faced opposition from university leaders concerned about rising operating costs and declining overseas enrolment.
However, the government reaffirmed its plans on October 19, 2026, when Education Minister Josh MacAlister told Parliament that the revenue would support England's higher education and skills system.
Responding to a parliamentary question about the policy's economic justification, MacAlister said the government had already conducted consultations and published an impact assessment in 2025, with an updated analysis expected shortly.
ADVERTISEMENT
He also maintained that planned increases in domestic tuition fee caps could generate around £6 billion for higher education providers over five years, compared with the levy's projected cost to universities of less than £1 billion over the same period.
How the international student levy will work
Under the proposal, universities in England will pay £925 annually for each international student, with the first 220 overseas enrolments exempt from the charge.
The levy will cover both new and existing students, with a university enrolling 1,000 international students facing an annual charge of £721,500 after the 220-student exemption.
The Office for Students will oversee its implementation using enrolment data, while the government intends to adjust the rate annually in line with inflation.
ADVERTISEMENT
Official projections indicate that the levy will generate £445 million ($594 million) in 2028–2029, rising to £465 million ($621 million) in 2029–2030 and £480 million ($641 million) in 2030–2031.
What the levy means for international students
The policy will affect universities recruiting from China, India, Nigeria, Pakistan and Bangladesh, alongside African markets such as Ghana, Kenya, Zimbabwe and South Africa.
Home Office figures show that China received 86,368 sponsored study visas in the year ending June 2026, followed by India with 82,523 and Nigeria with 26,060.
Pakistan recorded 19,600 adult student visas, while Bangladesh received about 8,800 over the same period.
ADVERTISEMENT
According to the Department for Education, students from India generated £5.3 billion in UK higher education export revenue in 2024, compared with £4.9 billion from China and £1.7 billion from Nigeria.
Overall, international higher education students generated an estimated £23.9 billion in export revenue for Britain that year.
Although students will not pay the levy directly, universities could pass on additional costs through higher international tuition fees, adding to the financial requirements already facing overseas applicants.
Birmingham City University has already raised fees for continuing international students by 2% for the 2026–2027 academic year, with a further 3.5% increase planned for 2027–2028.
Meanwhile, the University of Bath has advised overseas students who began their courses in 2026 to budget for annual tuition fee increases of up to 8%.
ADVERTISEMENT
International students at a UK university. British universities face a proposed £925 annual levy on international enrolments from August 2028. Source: Study Abroad Foundation — University of Manchester.
Universities question financial impact
The measure comes as British universities face tighter immigration rules and declining international recruitment, raising concerns about their financial sustainability.
Business Insider Africa previously reported that some British universities had withdrawn admission offers to Nigerian, Pakistani and Bangladeshi applicants over concerns about breaching stricter visa sponsorship requirements.
The financial strain has also affected the University of Sunderland, which is seeking to cut £40 million ($53 million) from its annual operating costs amid weaker international recruitment.
ADVERTISEMENT
Vivienne Stern, chief executive of Universities UK, questioned the government's revenue forecasts in comments reported by The i Paper.
“It is a daft policy, and that is evident from the way that international recruitment trends have been unfolding this autumn,” she said.
“The Government’s projections about the income it will raise are already unrealistic.”

title: Build Your Own Reasoning Model: A Full Video Course
content:
Discover more from Ahead of AI
Ahead of AI focuses on machine learning and AI research and is read by more than 200,000 researchers and practitioners who want to stay ahead in a rapidly evolving field.
Over 224,000 subscribers
Subscribe
By subscribing, you agree to Substack's Terms of Use, and acknowledge its Information Collection Notice and Privacy Policy.
Already have an account? Sign in
Building Reasoning Models from the Ground Up: A Full Video Course
Eight videos and over 11 hours of coding, covering evaluation, inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation in Python and PyTorch.
SEBASTIAN RASCHKA, PHD
OCT 24, 2026
310
12
34
Share
I have written a lot about reasoning models here over the last two years on Ahead of AI, including a recent article on mechanisms to control reasoning effort levels in contemporary LLMs. Reasoning models are still as relevant as ever. In fact, almost all current-generation LLMs today are reasoning models or offer a reasoning mode.
For those who are interested in how reasoning models work, including inference scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation, I wrote my recent Build Reasoning Model (From Scratch), which implements these from the ground up in PyTorch, which, in my experience, is still the best way to understand and learn how things really work.
Now, in the last few months, I also sat down and recorded accompanying lectures I wanted to share with you. So, below, you will find eight reasoning model-from-scratch coding videos (11 hours of content).
We start with a pre-trained LLM and implement methods to evaluate and improve it in Python and PyTorch. So, if you enjoyed my Coding LLMs from the Ground Up course last year, this is essentially the sequel (but you can also watch it without the prior course as a prerequisite).
I’m currently taking a short break and will be back soon with more exciting LLM research roundups next month. In the meantime, I hope you enjoy coding along!
How LLMs, reasoning models, and agents relate and fit together
As a small side note, and since I often get asked how reasoning models relate to today’s AI agents, here’s a short section on this before getting started with the videos.
A reasoning model is essentially an upgrade from a conventional LLM, that is, adding more post-training via reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (and optionally inference scaling techniques) to make it more capable of solving more challenging problems. Classically, reasoning models are developed for math and code, but the capabilities can generalize to other problem domains as well.
A reasoning model then functions as the engine inside an agent harness, where the agent harness is a software or tooling framework around the LLM/reasoning model to tackle even more challenging problems (bigger coding tasks, travel booking, and all other sorts of personal assistant tasks). The task of the harness is sophisticated context management and giving the LLM access to tools.
Figure 1: An engine analogy for conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agent harnesses. Figure from my Components of a Coding Agent article.
In this analogy depicted in the figure above, the model is the engine, and the agent harness adds the machinery that lets us use it for various things (as an upgrade from a simple chatbot interface). An agent can use either a conventional LLM or a reasoning model, but reasoning models are the more typical choice as they are more capable. (As mentioned above, most current-gen LLMs are reasoning models with variable reasoning effort settings.)
So, the bottom line is that reasoning models, as the “engine,” remain an important part of understanding modern LLM agents.
The resources accompanying these topics shown above are:
The Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) book and videos
The Build A Reasoning Model (From Scratch) book (and videos below)
The Components of a Coding Agent article on Substack
The videos below focus on developing the reasoning model that can power such a system.
Scope and prerequisites
The reasoning-from-scratch videos focus on a small pre-trained Qwen3 model, where we implement the reasoning methods ourselves in Python and PyTorch. Starting with a pre-trained model lets us focus on the interesting part: evaluation, inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation.
Regarding the prerequisites, I recommend being comfortable with Python and PyTorch. I designed the reasoning materials as standalone content, so the previous Build A Large Language Model (From Scratch) content is recommended but not strictly required.
Compute-resource-wise, you can work through the early text-generation and evaluation examples on a CPU. For the later experiments, especially training, a GPU makes the work much more practical. The first video covers the setup and some more recommendations; the repository also includes hardware and environment recommendations.
Figure 2: An overview of the topics being covered.
The companion book
These videos accompany my book, Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch). If you like to read through the explanation in more detail and at your own pace, work through exercises, and so on, I recommend the book as a companion here.
For the most in-depth learning experience, my suggestion is to read a chapter, work through its code alongside the corresponding video, and then try the exercises.
The book is available from Manning and Amazon, and the print edition is in color!
Figure 3: A random excerpt from the Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch) print book.
Thank you to everyone who has picked up a copy or recommended it to a friend. Your support helps me keep creating these materials.
The videos
As a last, quick side note before getting to the main videos below: For a shorter, more conceptual overview, I also recommend my AI Reasoning Models course on LinkedIn Learning (it should be free for 24h when accessing it via the link there, which shouldn’t then require a LinkedIn Premium subscription).
The course is about 90 minutes and explains how reasoning models work, covering the main ideas behind inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation. It’s a good optional preview if you’d like the main ideas without working through the full implementations below.
To get to the main part of this article, here are the eight main lecture videos.
1. Motivation and code setup
The first video starts with an explanation of the relationship between conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agents. Next, the main topic of the video is setting up the coding environment. This includes installing the Python and PyTorch dependencies (with uv), among others. I also discuss hardware choices and common setup issues.
Topics covered
The relationship between conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agent harnesses
On the benefits of learning through code implementations
The scope of this video series
Installing Python dependencies
Choosing hardware and checking CUDA or Apple Silicon support
Using a remote GPU with VS Code and troubleshooting the environment
Watch video 1 · Setup instructions
2. Loading a base model, text generation, and KV caching
Before adding reasoning methods in the upcoming videos, we need a working base model. Instead of training it from scratch, since that would be a whole other book (see Build A Large Language Model (From Scratch)), we start with a pre-trained model.
Here, we load the pre-trained weights of a Qwen3 0.6B model. Then, we implement the text-generation process via a streaming text generator and add KV caching and model compilation to make text generation more efficient.
These implementations give us the baseline and base components we will evaluate and improve in the following videos.
Topics covered
Encoding text as tokens and decoding it back into text
Downloading Qwen3 weights and loading the model on the selected compute device
Going over tensor shapes, logits, and next-token predictions
Implementing greedy decoding and streaming text generation
Handling end-of-sequence tokens and measuring generation speed
Adding a KV cache to reuse attention keys and values
Combining KV caching with torch.compile and comparing hardware performance
Watch video 2 · Chapter 2 code
3. Building a verifier for evaluation and reinforcement learning
In this lecture, we build a math-answer verifier step by step, from answer extraction to normalization and checking mathematical equivalence. We then use it to evaluate the model on MATH-500.
We use this verifier to evaluate the base model’s performance on the MATH-500 evaluation dataset.
However, the verifier also has a second job later in the series: providing the reward signal for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR).
Topics covered
Intro to verifiers and how they fit into LLM evaluation methods (other methods are covered in the book’s appendix)
Reusing answer verification as a reward signal for RLVR (more on that in chapter 6)
The verifier flow, including extracting final answers, normalizing answers and checking mathematical equivalence
Building an answer grader and an evaluation loop for MATH-500
Comparing base and reasoning models on MATH-500
Watch video 3 · Chapter 3 code
4. Inference-time scaling: sampling and self-consistency
Now we explore ways to improve answers while keeping the model weights fixed. But before implementing specific inference-scaling techniques, we first implement methods to generate diverse answers from the same prompt (this is standard practice in proprietary LLM chatbots, such as ChatGPT).
Concretely, we implement temperature scaling, multinomial sampling, and top-p filtering to generate diverse responses. Then we combine multiple responses through self-consistency, using majority voting over their final answers.
We also examine the tradeoff between answer accuracy and the extra computation needed to generate more candidates.
Topics covered
Comparing how additional compute benefits model performance during training and during inference
A gentle intro to inference-scaling through chain-of-thought prompts
Implementing temperature scaling and multinomial sampling to generate diverse answers
Adding top-p filtering to control the quality of the diverse answers
Combining candidate answers through self-consistency, one of the most popular inference scaling techniques
Evaluating MATH-500 accuracy against the cost of additional inference compute
Watch video 4 · Chapter 4 code
5. Inference-time scaling: scoring and self-refinement
Building on the previous video, we implement scoring functions to compare multiple answers generated from the same prompt. We can also use these scoring methods to break ties in self-consistency (covered in the previous lecture).
The scoring methods covered here include computing token and sequence log probabilities (this will also be relevant in the later reinforcement learning chapters). We then implement a self-refinement loop in which the model critiques an answer and attempts a revision.
The evaluation lets us check how useful those additional steps are for our model.
Topics covered
Using scoring functions for comparing multiple answers and breaking ties
Implementing a simple heuristic scorer
Computing token probabilities and sequence likelihoods (also relevant for the following lectures)
Using log probabilities for improved numerical stability
Building a self-refinement loop for generating critiques and revised answers
Evaluating self-refinement on MATH-500
Watch video 5 · Chapter 5 code
6. Reinforcement learning: implementing GRPO for RLVR
In this lecture, we move on to implementing a training technique called Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR). We first implement a simplified version of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), generate groups of responses, score them with our verifier, and use their relative rewards for the model weight updates during training.
Topics covered
Generating reasoning traces and understanding the relationship between answer lengths and problem-solving abilities
Discussion and comparison of two important LLM post-training methods: Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF) and Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR)
Turning verifier scores into rewards and relative advantages
Computing sequence log probabilities and a simplified GRPO loss
Assembling the training loop with logging and checkpoint saves
Evaluating checkpoints and checking training stability and memory needs
Watch video 6 · Chapter 6 code
7. Reinforcement learning: tracking, clipped policy ratios, and KL terms
Now that we implemented the training loop in the previous lecture, we can revisit it and analyze the training runs in more detail.
Concretely, this video adds more training metrics for inspection and analysis, including entropy and advantage statistics, clipped policy ratios, KL loss term values, and formatted rewards.
We then review the training logs and evaluation results to understand what these additions do and whether additions such as clipped policy ratios and KL loss terms are helpful.
Topics covered
Running longer training experiments and interpreting their logs
Tracking advantages and entropy to understand training behavior
Implementing clipping in the policy loss and analyzing its effects
Adding a KL loss term and discussing reward hacking
Understanding limitations of the simplified KL formulation
Implementing format rewards and conditioning them on answer correctness
Comparing checkpoints on MATH-500 and exploring further GRPO research
Watch video 7 · Chapter 7 code
8. Distilling a reasoning model
Finally, we explore another way to train a small reasoning model, that is, learning from answers generated by a stronger (and bigger) teacher model. We discuss different forms of distillation, prepare reasoning data, and implement the supervised training loop.
We finish this lecture and course by evaluating the distilled model on MATH-500 and comparing the results. This rounds out the series with an alternative to developing reasoning capabilities through reinforcement learning.
Topics covered
Comparing the different combination and approaches to distillation, including soft and hard distillation, and on-policy and off-policy distillation
Creating and collecting teacher-generated answers for the MATH dataset (using DeepSeek R1)
Preparing the distillation dataset, including tokenization and training/validation/test splits
Computing answer-token log probabilities and understanding the cross-entropy loss
Implementing supervised training and tracking training and validation losses
Evaluating checkpoints on MATH-500 and comparing distillation results
Watch video 8 · Chapter 8 code
Final words
As you watch these lectures, I encourage you to pause occasionally and try a small experiment of your own if something interesting comes to mind.
For example, feel free to change the sampling settings, inspect a few failed answers, or try variations of dif

title: Oldest GUI application that still runs on Windows 11 · enlyth
content:
Oldest GUI application that still runs on Windows 11
26 October 2026
·
2 min read
#windows
#gui
Early investigation
For a while I’ve been wondering about a silly question, which is, what’s the oldest application with a GUI that will still run on Windows 11 without modifications or emulation.
Given Windows’ excellent backwards compatibility, I expected the answer to be something impressively old.
Sadly, Windows 11 can’t run 16-bit Windows programs by itself, because 64-bit Windows has no NTVDM, so we’re going to have to find something from the early NT era.
I remember asking this question a while ago on an anonymous forum, where someone pointed me to Win32s, and suggested to find an early release version of it with FREECELL.exe.
So I did exactly that, and lo and behold, FREECELL.EXE with a date modified of 22-Feb-93 running and fully playable, without any changes on the latest version of Windows 11:
At the time of this post, that’s a 33 years and 8 months old application, which is impressively almost as old as me.
So I kinda thought “cool”, considered this a solved mystery and forgot about it shortly afterwards. But for some reason, this question popped into my mind again lately and this time I decided to dig deeper to see if I can find something older.
Further efforts
Digging through old Windows versions on the Internet Archive, I found some early NT 3.1 pre-release versions that seemed promising, but the main issue seemed to be either incompatibility with today’s executable format or API changes that came later in development.
The earliest 1991 versions used a draft PE format not compatible with modern Windows, and builds up to mid-1992 assumed the cdecl calling convention instead of stdcall for Windows API calls, so arguments would get removed twice, as such:
push hwnd          ; 4 bytes of args
call [ShowWindow]  ; Win11 ShowWindow is stdcall, ends with "ret 4" and removes them
add  esp, 4        ; the 1992 caller removes them again
Which would understandably cause the program to crash.
There was one application that caught my eye though, from Build 347, and that was CDPLAYER.EXE, linked on 16-Nov-1992. By then the calling convention was fixed, but the other programs in that build crash in their bundled C runtime. CDPLAYER.EXE avoids that by using the system’s crtdll.dll, and Windows 11 still ships a crtdll.dll in SysWOW64.
If you start the program, you get something like this:
That is because, duh, my computer doesn’t have a CD-ROM drive. But you can use a small DLL (cdemu.dll) to emulate one with some fake audio data and actually get it to play audio:
Pretty cool for a program that’s almost 34 years old!
What if we cheat?
So earlier I mentioned that 16-bit programs are out of the picture because they are no longer supported.
But if you want, you can use something like otvdm to run older Windows applications.
Behold, a fully playable version of REVERSI.EXE dated 15-Nov-1985 running on Windows 11, taken from Windows 1.01:
And although using otvdm does feel like cheating, I thought it was cool enough to include in this post.
